country_setting: global (multinational); online survey
N_total: responses 2,955 ; included after applying exclusion criteria 1,352
population_description: Adults (18 years and older) with and without COVID-19-related chemosensory impairment who had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose, recruited globally by convenience sampling through a multilingual online survey (responses collected May 2022 to August 2023)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (survey questions on smell and taste changes before and after each vaccine dose; distorted taste assessed as a single category)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Pre-vaccination distorted taste reported by 380 participants (of 1,352 included); 2% or fewer reported new onset of distorted taste following vaccination; approximately half of the cohort reported pre-existing COVID-19-related chemosensory dysfunction (composite smell/taste) prior to vaccination
onset_timing: Among the 75 participants who reported the timing and duration of post-vaccination chemosensory changes, approximately two-thirds indicated that the onset occurred on the day following vaccination (composite chemosensory changes)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Most of the 75 participants reporting post-vaccination chemosensory changes reported symptom duration longer than 1 month (<12wk — not >=12wk persistence; composite chemosensory)
special_populations_notes: pregnancy/lactation: participants who were pregnant after the COVID outbreak were excluded (n = 69), pregnancy being a known modulator of chemosensory ability; children: participants younger than 18 years were excluded (n = 33)
funding_conflicts: Funding: Liang-Dar Hwang is supported by an Australian Research Council Early Discovery Researcher Award (DE240100014); Conflicts: Kathrin Ohla works at dsm-firmenich, the company had no influence on the study design or interpretation of results; the other authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Vaccination is the exposure, not an intervention tested for taste dysfunction — Q3 block left blank per R6. Among participants with pre-existing qualitative impairments, improvement in distorted taste was reported by 12%–21% depending on vaccine dose and worsening by 3% or fewer (post-vaccination change, not natural-history recovery). Proposed mechanisms (transient inflammatory responses within the olfactory neuroepithelium, immune-mediated effects of residual viral material) are olfactory/general and not extended to taste: general/olfactory mechanism not taste-extended — not Q2-coded

country_setting: Panama; San Miguelito Health Region surveillance records and telephone follow-up
population_description: COVID-19-positive patients over five years of age followed by the San Miguelito Health Region, Panama, from July 7, 2021 through November 2, 2022; unvaccinated patients and patients whose recorded doses were exclusively Pfizer-BioNTech were included
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (self-reported clinical information collected by physicians during telephone follow-up calls)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Ageusia was reported by 507 patients (9.48%)
special_populations_notes: children: patients over five years of age were eligible; diabetes: diabetes recorded in 464 patients (8.68%); CKD: chronic kidney disease recorded in 14 patients (0.26%); immunocompromised: immunosuppression counted among the recorded chronic conditions
funding_conflicts: Conflicts: in compliance with the ICMJE uniform disclosure form, all authors declared that there are no other relationships or activities that could appear to have influenced the submitted work; funding not reported
extractor_notes: Vaccination dose category is the exposure, not an intervention tested for taste dysfunction — Q3 block left blank per R6. Exposure and outcomes were assessed from the same follow-up record; the timing of vaccination relative to infection could not be established (authors' limitation)

country_setting: Brazil; university research laboratory (Cesumar University, Maringá, Paraná), participants recruited from hospital-discharge referrals
population_description: Post-COVID-19 individuals aged 18 to 65 years with a confirmed diagnosis of COVID-19 through a qualitative molecular test (RT-PCR), recruited from hospital-discharge referrals; 67.7% had been hospitalized and 34.8% required ICU admission during acute infection
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (standardized questionnaire; anosmia and ageusia not assessed by objective olfactometry or gustometry, per authors' limitation)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Ageusia (n = 121) vs no ageusia (n = 80) of 201 participants (Table 3)
pathogenesis_finding: Alterations involving both smell and taste may correlate with neurological symptoms, likely reflecting involvement of the central nervous system and persistent dysfunction of the olfactory pathway (authors' discussion)
special_populations_notes: diabetes: diabetes mellitus recorded in 32 participants (15.9%)
funding_conflicts: Funding: the Article Processing Charge was funded by the Coordenação de Aperfeiçoamento de Pessoal de Nível Superior - Brasil (CAPES); Conflicts: the authors declare no competing interests
extractor_notes: No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6. Table 3 prints duration-type bands under the ageusia group (<2 months n = 93; 2–4 months n = 11; 4–6 months n = 5; >6 months n = 14) in a VO2peak comparison; the text does not unambiguously define these as persistence bands, so they are not coded as >=12wk persistence

country_setting: USA; University of Iowa COVID-19 cohort and NIH All of Us Research Program COVID-19 cohort
N_total: UI cohort 187 ; All of Us (AoU) cohort 947
population_description: Individuals with COVID-19 and whole-genome sequencing data, classified as cases or controls by self-reported loss of smell and/or taste phenotypes (UI cohort recruited at the University of Iowa; AoU cohort from the NIH All of Us Research Program)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (binary loss-of-taste phenotype from cohort records/survey)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: UI cohort (N = 187): 95 cases and 92 controls for the loss of taste phenotype; 8 participants reported only a loss of taste and 87 reported a loss in smell and taste. AoU cohort (N = 947): 421 cases and 526 controls for loss of smell or taste (composite phenotype)
pathogenesis_finding: The most probable cause of the loss of taste with COVID-19 is the viral invasion of gustatory nerves, taste receptor cells, and the olfactory epithelium, with proposed contributing factors including an increase in pro-inflammatory cytokines leading to damage of associated cells; the paper also distinguishes true loss of taste from loss of flavor due to olfactory dysfunction
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: University of Iowa Interdisciplinary Genetics T32 Predoctoral Training Grant (grant number T32 GM008629), the Integrated DNA Technologies Bioinformatics Fellowship Program, and University of Iowa Stead Family Department of Pediatrics funds; Conflicts: the authors have declared that no competing interests exist
extractor_notes: Genetic association / machine-learning study sampled by symptom status (case-control), so prevalence is by-design per R2. Confirmation routes differed (UI cohort: antibody or PCR testing, or presumed positive as a symptomatic household contact) — mixed per R7(e). No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6

country_setting: Denmark; questionnaire cohort (Aarhus University Hospital / Odense University Hospital research units)
population_description: Individuals with sudden chemosensory dysfunction (CD) during the COVID-19 pandemic, enrolled from 2 April 2020 with repeated questionnaires and re-surveyed four years after symptom onset; median age at enrolment 46 years (range: 18–87)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (validated self-report questionnaire items on chemosensory dysfunction and recovery; gustatory dysfunction (GD) assessed within composite CD)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported for taste specifically (cohort enrolled on the basis of sudden chemosensory dysfunction; most participants reported combined olfactory and gustatory dysfunction, Table 2)
onset_timing: Sudden chemosensory dysfunction during the COVID-19 pandemic; mean time from symptom onset to the baseline questionnaire was 82 days (IQR: 28–103)
recovery_complete_as_printed: Full recovery from CD (composite smell/taste) reported by 43% of participants after four years; full GD recovery reported by 59% of male and 51% of female participants (p = 0.028)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Participants reporting partial recovery or no improvement formed the persistent CD group at four years after symptom onset; persistent dysfunction was most common among participants aged 45–59 years (68%)
pathogenesis_finding: Reported taste loss may reflect impaired flavour perception rather than true gustatory dysfunction, as subjective olfactory loss may not align with objective testing (authors' limitation discussion)
special_populations_notes: none reported
follow_up_duration: mean follow-up 1,496 days (IQR: 1,398–1,616); questionnaire four years after symptom onset
funding_conflicts: Funding: none; Conflicts: AWF reports financial support from or interest in Region Midtjyllands Sundhedsvidenskabelige Forskningsfond, Folkeuniversitetet; all authors have submitted the ICMJE Form for Disclosure of Potential Conflicts of Interest
extractor_notes: Outcomes are reported mainly for composite chemosensory dysfunction (CD); GD-specific recovery is printed only split by sex. Confirmation mixed: full recovery was compared between participants reporting a positive PCR test (n = 221) and those with no positive PCR (n = 135, including negative tests or no test results). No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6

country_setting: Hong Kong SAR, China; community-recruited cohort (Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
population_description: Adults who had recovered from SARS-CoV-2 (confirmed by conversion from positive to negative rapid antigen (lateral flow) test or PCR test), recruited from the community and grouped by time since viral clearance: Group 1 (3 months), Group 2 (6 months), Group 3 (12 months); mean age 59.9 ± 8.6 years
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (ODOFIN Taste Strips 50, 16-strip test; hypogeusia identified by a test score lower than 9)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Hypogeusia at Visit 1 in 27 (22.5%) of 120 participants
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Hypogeusia in 18 (15.0%) at Visit 2, three months after Visit 1 (participants enrolled at 3, 6 or 12 months post–viral clearance)
taste_score_change_as_printed: Whole cohort (n = 120): a two-way ANOVA revealed no significant main effect of recovery group or within-group differences on ODOFIN scores between Visit 1 and Visit 2; gustatory function had largely normalised at the first visit across all groups and remained stable at follow-up
pathogenesis_finding: Gustatory dysfunction may arise from viral replication within taste receptor cells, evidenced by SARS-CoV-2 co-localisation with type II taste cell markers and the ACE2 receptor within taste buds (cited evidence discussed by the authors)
special_populations_notes: none reported
follow_up_duration: two visits three months apart; longest observation 15 months post–viral clearance (Group 3)
funding_conflicts: Funding: Health and Medical Research Fund (HMRF) - Commissioned Research on COVID-19 from the Health Bureau of Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (reference number COVID19030); Conflicts: the authors declare no competing interests
extractor_notes: No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6. Plasma biomarkers (e.g. alpha-synuclein) correlated with olfactory, not gustatory, function (no significant correlations between alpha-synuclein and gustatory function at either visit), so no additional taste mechanism is coded

country_setting: USA; Indiana University School of Dentistry / IU School of Medicine COVID-19 Research Registry
N_total: long COVID cohort recruited 42 ; scRNA-seq subset: LC-D 6 ; healthy controls 6
population_description: Adults aged 18 years and older with long COVID and a history of a SARS-CoV-2-positive laboratory (RT-PCR) test, recruited via the IU School of Medicine COVID-19 Research Registry; the scRNA-seq group (LC-D) comprised six individuals with impaired bitter taste scores (WETT bitter score ≤1), compared with six healthy controls from pre-COVID cryopreserved saliva samples
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (Waterless Empirical Taste Test, WETT; subjects with WETT scores < 2 considered dysgeusic)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: not reported (sampling conditional on taste dysfunction status for the mechanistic comparison)
pathogenesis_finding: Single-cell transcriptomes of salivary epithelial cells from individuals with bitter taste dysfunction (LC-D) showed downregulation of genes involved in cytoskeletal dynamics and taste cell–nerve synapse assembly, reduced Type II and III taste receptor genes critical for bitter taste perception, and downregulated microbial defense markers TLR2 and TLR4, suggesting chronic inflammation and sustained dysregulated epithelial turnover
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: support from Delta Dental Research Program to MS, grant number #44-762-54; Conflicts: the authors declare no conflicts of interest; the funders had no role in the design of the study
extractor_notes: Mechanistic human study; enrolment for the transcriptomic comparison was conditional on persistent bitter taste dysfunction in long COVID (by-design sampling, R2). No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6

country_setting: Bosnia and Herzegovina; University of Sarajevo (Institute for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology)
N_total: volunteers 100 ; individuals with confirmed virus infection (abstract) 96 ; dysfunction (OGD) group 50 ; no-OGD group 50
population_description: Unrelated, nonconsanguineous healthy adult volunteers (age over 18 years, no chronic diseases) with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection in the past year (confirmed by a primary care physician after the PCR test), divided into a group with olfactory/gustatory dysfunction (OGD) and a group without dysfunction (no-OGD)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (questionnaire adapted from MCSTQ-Sc, with sections on past SARS-CoV-2 infection and smell and/or taste disorders)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: participants were divided into groups according to the presence of self-reported taste dysfunction (OGD group 50; no-OGD group 50); no population prevalence printed
pathogenesis_theories: T1; T2; T5; T11 (host genetic variation in taste signalling genes HCN4, PLCB2, TAS1R1)
pathogenesis_finding: Statistically significant differences between taste-dysfunction groups were observed for HCN4 variants c.*2393C>G (p = 0.013) and c.2556G>A (p = 0.026), PLCB2 variants c.3037-55T>C (p = 0.019) and c.582+958_582+959inv (p = 0.021), and TAS1R1 variant c.1594+41G>A (p = 0.03), indicating a possible genetic association with taste dysfunction in response to virus infection
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: grant of the Ministry of Science, Higher Education and Youth of Sarajevo Canton (contract no.: 27-02-11-41250-40/21); Conflicts: the authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Genetic association study; group allocation was by olfactory/gustatory dysfunction (OGD) status, a composite, although the genetic analysis targets taste dysfunction (dysgeusia). Proposed mechanisms in the discussion: smell and taste disorders likely arise due to primary damage to olfactory sensory neurons and taste buds, mainly mediated by infection, inflammation, and subsequent dysfunction of supporting nonneuronal cells in the mucosa; taste receptor cells are highly susceptible to inflammatory processes including the cytokine storm of COVID-19. No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6

country_setting: Austria, Germany and Switzerland; general population online survey
N_total: respondents submitted 3,028 ; complete responses analysed 2,340 (Austria 1,023 ; Germany 1,031 ; Switzerland 286)
population_description: Non-institutionalised adults (18 years and older) residing in Austria, Germany and Switzerland, recruited in January 2025 via an online panel; respondents completed the culturally adapted and validated Smell-Qx questionnaire on smell and taste disorders (SATDs), aetiology and quality of life
taste_measurement: patient-reported scale named (Smell-Qx questionnaire)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Taste impairment reported by 442 (18.9%) of 2,340 respondents (Austria 168 (16.4%); Germany 197 (19.1%); Switzerland 77 (26.9%))
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: 54.3% (n = 230) of respondents with taste loss reported no improvement or worsening of 'taste' loss since onset (status at survey, January 2025; no standardised time band printed)
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: funding was received via the Rosetrees Trust; Conflicts: the authors have no conflicts of interest to declare
extractor_notes: General-population SATD survey, not an infection-confirmed cohort: of respondents providing a suspected aetiology (n = 454), all indicated symptoms began following an acute upper respiratory tract infection; causes were self-attributed. No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6; no taste-specific pathogenesis content — Q2 blank

country_setting: Spain; university clinical hospitals (Virgen de la Arrixaca University Clinical Hospital, Murcia)
N_total: original pool 201 ; included in the analysis 104
population_description: Adults with polymerase chain reaction–confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection during the first and second pandemic waves, sampled in the post-acute phase approximately 75 days after diagnosis, when nasal and/or oropharyngeal swabs were obtained to quantify expression of SARS-CoV-2 entry-related genes (ACE2, TMPRSS2, furin, NRP1)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (presence or absence of dysgeusia recorded as a binary clinical variable)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Dysgeusia was reported by 36.5% (n = 38) of participants; 63.5% (n = 66) denied gustatory symptoms
onset_timing: not reported (detailed information regarding symptom onset, duration, or progression during the acute phase was not collected)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Dysgeusia present in 36.5% (n = 38) at sampling approximately 75 days after diagnosis (<12wk — not >=12wk persistence)
pathogenesis_finding: Persistent expression levels of SARS-CoV-2 entry-related genes (furin, ACE2, NRP1, and TMPRSS2) in nasal or oropharyngeal swab samples during the post-acute phase are not significantly associated with olfactory dysfunction or dysgeusia
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: this research received no external funding; Conflicts: the authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6

design: cross-sectional | longitudinal prospective cohort study (paper's wording); the reported analysis is baseline data, described by the authors as a cross-sectional single-cohort study
country_setting: USA; Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, Columbus
population_description: Sixty subjects aged 27–78 years with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC / long COVID) and persistent symptoms lasting 4.3–52.9 months (median 27.48 months), who had contracted COVID-19 between 17 January 2020 and 21 December 2023
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (modified NIH Toolbox taste test) plus self-reported taste dysfunction
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Self-reported taste dysfunction in 63.6% (35/55 tested); objectively confirmed taste impairment on the modified NIH Toolbox taste test in 16% (9/55; also printed as 16.4% (9/55))
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Cohort enrolled with symptoms persisting 4.3–52.9 months (median 27.48 months) after infection; confirmed taste impairment in 16% (9/55) at assessment
pathogenesis_finding: 64% of subjects reported taste dysfunction but only 16% displayed deficits in taste identification — a discrepancy the authors attribute to confusion between flavor (mediated in part by olfaction) and taste; strong associations were found between the identification components of smell and taste tests (p = 0.003), which may involve more central processing, but not with threshold tests
special_populations_notes: pregnancy/lactation: current pregnancy was an exclusion criterion
follow_up_duration: not reported (follow-up testing at 3-, 6-, 9- and 12-month intervals was a stated future goal)
funding_conflicts: Conflicts: author ACM serves as CMO and on Board of Directors for Otologic Technologies and is a paid consultant for Amgen; funding not reported (acknowledgements: none)
extractor_notes: No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6. Design conflict flagged per R1(a): the paper labels the study a longitudinal prospective cohort, but the reported taste data are a single baseline assessment and the authors themselves describe the analysis as cross-sectional

country_setting: Japan; Kanagawa Cancer Center Hospital, Yokohama (hospital inpatients)
N_total: patients admitted with COVID-19 520 ; met inclusion and exclusion criteria 95 ; analysed 52 (group A 26 ; group B 26)
population_description: Patients admitted with acute COVID-19 to Kanagawa Cancer Center between September 13, 2021 and September 30, 2023, stratified by the presence (group A) or absence (group B) of dysosmia and/or dysgeusia at admission; group B was matched to group A for age, disease severity and cancer status
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (chief complaint of dysgeusia at admission, confirmed by the attending physician)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: group A (dysosmia and/or dysgeusia) n = 26 and group B (neither symptom) n = 26 by design; dysgeusia specifically (Table 3, by vaccination status): positive in 6 of 11 unvaccinated and 15 of 39 vaccinated patients
onset_timing: Dysgeusia/dysosmia present as chief complaints at admission during acute COVID-19; blood sampling at a mean of 4.69 ± 2.51 days after COVID-19 onset in group A vs 3.62 ± 2.22 days in group B
pathogenesis_theories: T5; T11 (kynurenine pathway activation with neurotoxic quinolinic acid accumulation)
pathogenesis_finding: Patients with dysosmia/dysgeusia (group A) showed significantly lower serum tryptophan [median 9.70 μg/mL vs 10.40, p = 0.031] and higher kynurenine–tryptophan ratio [61.34 vs 53.52, p < 0.037] and quinolinic acid levels [574.39 nM vs 443.65, p < 0.0169] than patients without these symptoms; the authors propose kynurenine-pathway activation (IDO induced by proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma) with quinolinic acid as a trigger/biomarker of dysosmia/dysgeusia
special_populations_notes: pregnancy/lactation: pregnant women were excluded; children: adolescents aged <20 years were excluded; pre-existing chemosensory disorder: patients with pre-existing taste or smell impairment were excluded
funding_conflicts: Funding: Kanagawa Prefecture Hospital Cancer Fund [grant number 2022CancerC358]; the funder had no role in the study design, collection, analysis or interpretation of data; Conflicts: Jun Tsukiji reports receiving a scholarship from Shionogi Pharma (the Kanagawa Prefecture Hospital Cancer Fund); the other authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Case-control stratification was by the composite dysosmia and/or dysgeusia; dysgeusia-specific counts are printed only by vaccination status (Table 3). No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6

country_setting: USA; National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2011–2014
population_description: US adults aged 40 years and older participating in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2011–2014 (pre-COVID-19 survey cycles); taste disorders identified through self-reported questionnaires and interviews
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (self-reported taste disorder in the past 12 months, questionnaire/interview)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Taste disorders had a prevalence of 5.1% (95% CI: 4.5–5.6)
special_populations_notes: diabetes: higher taste disorder rates in individuals with a history of diabetes (7.3%; 95% CI: 5.8–8.7)
funding_conflicts: Funding: National Key Clinical Discipline, National Natural Science Foundation of China (82470696), Guangdong Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation (2024A1515010956), the program of Guangdong Provincial Clinical Research Center for Digestive Diseases (2020B1111170004), and Guangzhou Science and Technology Program (2024A04J6400); Conflicts: the authors declare no conflict of interest
extractor_notes: Population survey of taste disorders of any cause using pre-COVID-19 (2011–2014) data; no viral infection cohort and no taste-specific pathogenesis content — Q2 blank. No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6

country_setting: Germany; University Children's Hospital, Katholisches Klinikum Bochum (Ruhr University Bochum)
N_total: children examined 123 (noninfected controls 18 ; acute upper respiratory tract infection 34 ; acute SARS-CoV-2 infection 30 ; postinfection with persistent symptoms (PI+) 28 ; postinfection without persistent symptoms (PI−) 13)
population_description: Children and adolescents examined from 07/2021 to 10/2022 in five groups: acute SARS-CoV-2 infection (AC), acute other upper respiratory tract infection (URTI), postinfection with remaining symptoms ≥12 weeks after SARS-CoV-2 infection (PI+), postinfection without remaining symptoms (PI−), and noninfected controls (NI); group median ages 10–13 years
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (Taste Strips) plus questionnaire-based subjective impairment
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Severe hypogeusia (Taste Strips) was mostly in AC children (18%), followed by PI+ (12%) and PI− (10%); subjective taste impairment was most frequent in PI+ (29%), then AC (14%), vs ≤10% in all other groups
recovery_any_as_printed: In follow-up testing after a maximum period of 16 weeks (17 of the 64 acute-group children), two children with hypogeusia and a SARS-CoV-2 infection at baseline recovered, whereas 1 child with and 2 children without SARS-CoV-2 infection worsened substantially
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: PI+ group (remaining symptoms ≥12 weeks after SARS-CoV-2 infection): severe hypogeusia in 12% and subjective taste impairment in 29% at assessment
pathogenesis_finding: There is no consensus regarding the exact cause of hypogeusia; possible etiologies include neurologic damage, tissue hypoxia, immune or inflammatory reactions, and the authors speculate that infection with the virus causes damage to the second and third neurons of taste processing and disrupts the connection with centers of emotional processing such as the amygdala
special_populations_notes: children: the entire study population comprised children and adolescents (group median ages 10–13 years)
follow_up_duration: follow-up testing after a maximum period of 16 weeks in a subset of the acute groups
funding_conflicts: Funding: the authors have no funding or conflicts of interest to disclose; Conflicts: the authors have no funding or conflicts of interest to disclose
extractor_notes: Acute-group allocation was by SARS-CoV-2 PCR (examiners blinded to the result); postinfection groups were defined by infection history and symptom status, hence mixed confirmation. Group sizes as printed in the abstract and Table 1. No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6

country_setting: Turkey; Ankara Bilkent City Hospital (hospitalised patients)
N_total: hospitalised patients 96 (with new-onset olfactory and/or gustatory dysfunction 53 ; control subjects 43)
population_description: Hospitalised patients diagnosed with COVID-19 via polymerase chain reaction testing between September 2020 and January 2021; 53 patients with new-onset olfactory and/or gustatory dysfunction and 43 control subjects were selected through online randomization
taste_measurement: patient-reported scale named (Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores for symptom severity and recovery)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: taste loss was present in 44 (45.8%) of the 96 hospitalised patients (dysfunction and control groups were selected by symptom status through online randomization)
onset_timing: New-onset olfactory and/or gustatory dysfunction during acute COVID-19, assessed from the admission history
recovery_complete_as_printed: Complete recovery of gustatory dysfunction in 33 (75%) at the 90-day follow-up
recovery_any_as_printed: All patients with taste impairment recovered at 90 days (75% complete, 25% partial)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: No patient with taste impairment remained unrecovered at the 90-day follow-up (75% complete and 25% partial recovery)
pathogenesis_finding: Procalcitonin and CRP levels were significantly associated with the development of both olfactory and gustatory dysfunction (p < 0.05), and lower NLR, corrected NLR, NMR, and PLR values were strong predictors of recovery, linking systemic inflammatory markers to gustatory dysfunction and its recovery
special_populations_notes: pregnancy/lactation: pregnant or lactating patients were excluded; children: patients under 18 years of age were excluded
funding_conflicts: Funding: all authors have declared that no financial support was received from any organization for the submitted work (ICMJE disclosure); Conflicts: no conflicts of interest declared (ICMJE uniform disclosure form, as printed)
extractor_notes: No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6

country_setting: Saudi Arabia; online questionnaire (social media and healthcare networks)
population_description: Saudi residents aged 18 years and older (men and non-pregnant women) who had laboratory-confirmed mild-to-moderate COVID-19 and self-reported new-onset olfactory or gustatory dysfunction after COVID-19, recruited by convenience sampling through an online questionnaire
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (online questionnaire, originally developed and validated in English)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: sudden loss of taste was reported by 267 (70.8%) of the 377 included participants, all of whom were enrolled on the basis of new-onset olfactory or gustatory dysfunction after COVID-19
onset_timing: New-onset dysfunction that emerged during the acute infection (sudden loss of taste during COVID-19 infection); dysfunction arising solely after clinical recovery was excluded by the study definitions
special_populations_notes: pregnancy/lactation: pregnant women were excluded; pre-existing chemosensory disorder: individuals with pre-existing chemosensory disorders were excluded; diabetes: diabetes mellitus reported by 30.2% of the participants with comorbidities (n = 86)
funding_conflicts: Funding: this work was supported by the Deanship of Scientific Research, Vice Presidency for Graduate Studies and Scientific Research, King Faisal University, Saudi Arabia, 'KFU252640'; Conflicts: the authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6. The mechanistic discussion centres on olfactory pathways (parosmia/phantosmia) and is not extended to taste: general/olfactory mechanism not taste-extended — not Q2-coded

country_setting: Italy; University of Perugia / Azienda Ospedaliera Santa Maria della Misericordia, Perugia
N_total: women who had COVID-19 during pregnancy 13 ; controls (CTR) 10
population_description: Women who contracted COVID-19 during pregnancy (May 2021 to March 2022 period; inclusion required a positive test for SARS-CoV-2 infection), assessed more than 1 year after infection with a questionnaire on smell and taste disorders; cases had persistent alterations in taste and/or smell, compared with women whose disorders had resolved and with 10 controls
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (questionnaire investigating smell and taste disorders more than 1 year after the infection)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: one year after infection, of the 13 women who had COVID-19 during pregnancy, two women (15%) presented only taste disorder and one woman (7.7%) presented only smell disorder; five women (38%) had no alterations in taste or smell
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Taste and/or smell disorders still present more than 1 year post-infection defined the case group; two women (15%) presented only taste disorder at one year
pathogenesis_theories: T9; T11 (elevated acid sphingomyelinase degrading sphingomyelin, a myelin sheath component)
pathogenesis_finding: One year after SARS-CoV-2 infection, mothers with taste and smell disturbances had higher serum acid sphingomyelinase (aSMase) levels (51.54 ± 6.07 pg/mL) than those without taste and smell alterations (28.05 ± 4.57 pg/mL); aSMase degrades sphingomyelin, which is essential for the myelin sheath, and taste alteration has been correlated with myelin-related lesions in the central nervous system
special_populations_notes: pregnancy/lactation: all participants contracted COVID-19 during pregnancy and were assessed as new mothers one year after infection
funding_conflicts: Funding: this research was funded by Fondazione Cassa di Risparmio, grant number 20418 (2021.0348); Conflicts: the authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Pilot case-control study. Internal count note: the printed subgroup counts for the 13 women (only taste 2; only smell 1; no alterations 5) leave the remaining women (with both taste and smell disorders) without an explicit printed count in the text. No intervention tested — Q3 block left blank per R6

design: retrospective cohort | documentary and retrospective study (paper's wording)
country_setting: Brazil; hospital records dataset of the Paraíba State Department of Health
population_description: Older adults aged 60 years or older (mean age 74.50 ± 9.35 years) hospitalised with severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and a confirmed diagnosis of COVID-19 in Paraíba, Brazil; data extracted from individual hospital record sheets collected through a national form routinely applied in Brazilian hospitals
