taste_measurement: self-report symptom (interview) with self-reported severity scale 0-10 for taste; primary endpoint composite total recovery of taste and smell
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: 93% reported taste loss (enrolment conditional on chemosensory loss)
recovery_complete_as_printed: 249/714 (34.9%) reported total recovery of chemosensory function (composite taste and smell); 30.7% at 30-60 days, 44% at 61-90 days, 41.1% at more than 90 days since symptom onset
intervention: Drug therapies used for COVID-19 symptoms (observational exposures): systemic corticosteroids, oseltamivir, vitamin C, ibuprofen, hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine, azithromycin, ivermectin, nitazoxanide, anticoagulants, oral zinc
intervention_dose_course: not reported (doses and courses not stated)
N_per_arm: any treatment 437 ; no treatment 277 ; azithromycin 315 ; ivermectin 150 ; vitamin C 149 ; systemic corticosteroids 146 ; oral zinc 108 ; chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine 67 ; oseltamivir 56 ; nitazoxanide 27 ; anticoagulants 12 (per-drug counts as printed)
treatment_recovery_as_printed: Total recovery of taste and smell (composite): treated 122/437 (27.9%) vs untreated 127/277 (45.8%); no medication had a clear positive effect; oral zinc associated with lower chance of total recovery (OR 0.24, 95% CI 0.1-0.5); nitazoxanide trended to higher recovery (OR 3.30, 95% CI 1.35-8.20, not significant after Bonferroni correction)
adverse_events_as_printed: 55/483 (11.4%) of medication users reported adverse events; highest with chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine (22.4%), azithromycin (14.3%), oral zinc (13.9%); most common upper abdominal pain and nausea; 4 subjects (0.8%) had cardiac arrhythmia; no other severe adverse events reported
special_populations_notes: Comorbidities recorded including diabetes and hypothyroidism; hypothyroidism associated with lower total recovery (17.9%); no dose adjustments or contraindications reported
follow_up_duration: median 81 days (IQR 60-104) between symptom onset and interview
funding_conflicts: Funding: None; Conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest
extractor_notes: Virus confirmation mixed: 628 (95.2% of those with data) confirmed by RT-PCR or serology; others without test confirmation included on highly suspicious diagnosis by familial history or tomography findings (per R7e). Recovery endpoint is composite taste+smell total recovery, not taste-specific. Internal inconsistency: adverse-event denominator printed as 483 medication users vs 437 treated elsewhere; copied as printed. No taste-specific pathogenesis mechanism proposed; zinc olfactory harm discussion is smell-only - not Q2-coded per R5.

design: cross-sectional | online patient questionnaire survey (USA Smell and Taste Patient Survey) reported within a research-agenda paper
country_setting: United States; online survey (April 6-28, 2022)
N_total: completed survey 6,100 ; US residents 5,815 ; reported smell and/or taste loss 5,528 ; final analysed 4,877
virus: SARS-CoV-2 (74% of patients reported their disorder was due to COVID; remainder other/non-COVID etiologies)
population_description: Adults (18 years or older after cleaning) in the US with self-reported smell and/or taste loss, mostly from long COVID, who completed an online patient survey
taste_measurement: self-report symptom (patient-rated treatment efficacy categories: extremely/very/moderately/slightly/not effective at all)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: 79% reported ongoing dysfunction (composite smell/taste); average duration of ongoing dysfunction 3.65 years; for those who recovered, average duration of dysfunction was 1.47 years (composite as printed)
pathogenesis_finding: Paper states patients often report taste impairment when flavour is altered because olfactory stimulation occurs retro-nasally during ingestion, and notes a tendency to equate flavour (taste + smell) with taste
intervention: Patient-reported treatments used for chemosensory dysfunction: nasal steroids, oral steroids, zinc, nasal rinse, smell training, theophylline, alpha lipoic acid, omega-3, platelet-rich plasma (PRP)
intervention_dose_course: not reported (paper states complete information on duration of steroid use or olfactory training was not available; regimens varied)
N_per_arm: 1,890 reported using treatments; nasal steroids 43% and smell training 31% of treatment users; smell training users 790 (other per-treatment Ns not printed)
treatment_recovery_as_printed: Patient-rated efficacy (not recovery): nasal steroids rated slightly effective or not effective at all by 91% of those aged 40-60 and 93% of those 60+; smell training rated slightly/not effective by 91% of those 40-60 and 89% of those 60+; only those under 40 reported more than slight efficacy of steroids or smell training; age was the most consistent predictor of rated efficacy
special_populations_notes: Older adults: treatment efficacy rated significantly lower in those aged 40-60 and 60+ versus younger groups; paper notes older adults with olfactory impairment are at increased risk for Alzheimer's disease. Children under 18 were excluded from analysis (n=176 removed)
funding_conflicts: Funding: Supported by PCORI Engagement Contract EASC #00261 and NIH grant R01AG062006-05 from the National Institute on Aging; Conflicts: The authors have no conflicts to declare
extractor_notes: Mixed-etiology patient survey (COVID and non-COVID chemosensory disorders); outcomes are composite smell/taste and patient-rated treatment efficacy rather than taste-specific recovery, so recovery fields are 'not reported' per R3. Paper is a research-agenda/update article reporting an original survey (primary survey data extracted). Olfactory ageing/regeneration mechanisms discussed are smell-only - not Q2-coded per R5.

design: case series >=10 | 12-month observational pilot study (paper's wording)
country_setting: Italy; otolaryngology clinic, Fidenza Hospital, Parma
population_description: Adults aged 18 years or older with persistent post-COVID-19 hyposmia and dysgeusia presenting 30 days after COVID-19 resolution at an otolaryngology clinic, 2020-2021; 57.5% female
taste_measurement: patient-reported scale named (11-point visual analog scale, VAS 0-10, taste assessed separately from smell)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: all 87 patients enrolled with persistent post-COVID-19 dysgeusia (with hyposmia) - enrolment conditional on dysfunction
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Enrolled with persistent dysfunction 30 days after COVID-19 resolution; time from infection to treatment start: <=90 days 19 (21.8%) ; 91-180 days 16 (18.4%) ; 181-360 days 40 (46.0%) ; >360 days 12 (13.8%)
taste_score_change_as_printed: whole treated cohort: mean taste VAS 3.2 at treatment start (T0) to 7.1 at 12 months (T5), significant improvement between all time points (p<0.001); subgroup treated within 90 days of infection achieved mean taste VAS 8.58 at 12 months
pathogenesis_finding: Paper proposes gustatory loss may arise from indirect damage of taste receptors via infection of epithelial cells of the oral mucosa, and that excessive inflammatory response, endothelial dysfunction and microthrombus formation may damage the olfactory and gustatory epithelia
intervention: Combination protocol targeting inflammation and endothelial dysfunction: systemic corticosteroids (dexamethasone then prednisone), glycosaminoglycan-based antithrombotic mesoglycan, diuretic acetazolamide, and vitamin complex (plus omeprazole)
intervention_dose_course: Phase 1 (7 days, day hospital, daily): dexamethasone 8 mg IV; mesoglycan 30 mg IM; multivitamin complex (ascorbic acid, vitamins B1, B2, B6 in 100 mL physiological solution) IV; acetazolamide 250 mg orally; oral multivitamin complex with elevated zinc content (10 mg); omeprazole 40 mg IV. Phase 2 (30 days, home, oral): prednisone 5 mg for 3 days then 2.5 mg for 4 days; mesoglycan 50 mg capsule once daily for 30 days; multivitamin complex with elevated zinc for 30 days
N_per_arm: single arm 87 ; latency subgroups: A (<=90 days) 19 ; B (91-180 days) 16 ; C (181-360 days) 40 ; D (>360 days) 12
treatment_recovery_as_printed: No proportion with complete recovery printed; outcome reported as VAS score change (see taste_score_change): taste VAS improved progressively and significantly from T0 to 12 months, with earlier treatment start (<=90 days) associated with more pronounced recovery
adverse_events_as_printed: No safety problems were identified and the treatment was always well-tolerated (as printed)
special_populations_notes: Adults only (age <18 excluded); patients using anticoagulants excluded; patients aged >60 years were 7 (8.0%)
funding_conflicts: Funding: Neopharmed Gentili S.P.A. funded the medical writing assistance and article publication charges ('Neopharmed Gentili S.P.A funded this'); Conflicts: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist
extractor_notes: Single-arm treated cohort: recovery numbers recorded under treatment per R3. Virus confirmation: paper states prior resolved SARS-CoV-2 infection and clinical diagnosis of post-COVID-19 hyposmia/dysgeusia; COVID-19 serology and molecular testing performed before treatment were required to be negative (resolved infection) - original diagnostic route not stated, coded 'not reported'. Uncontrolled pre-post design coded case series >=10 per R1(c) despite 'observational pilot study' label.

country_setting: Poland; Institute of Physiology and Pathology of Hearing, Kajetany (specialist hearing/olfaction center)
population_description: Subjects aged 12-73 years (mean 41.9) presenting to the center for subjective olfactory dysfunction associated with COVID-19 that started during COVID-19 and lasted at least 1 month after acute symptoms subsided; 65 women, 16 men
taste_types_reported: unspecified taste dysfunction (abnormal Taste Strips result)
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (Taste Strips test, short version - sweet, salty, sour, bitter)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING (sample selected for olfactory dysfunction): abnormal taste result in 17% of subjects (as printed); Taste Strips scores: 4 points 59 (73%), 3 points 12 (15%), 2 points 5 (6%), 1 point 4 (5%), 0 points 1; correct recognition: sweet 96.3%, sour 88.9%, bitter 86.4%, salty 84%
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: not reported (cohort selected for olfactory dysfunction lasting at least 1 month; months since infection ranged 1-25, mean 8.3 months)
pathogenesis_finding: Paper states the mechanism of COVID-19 gustatory dysfunction is not thoroughly investigated but points to two possibilities: presence of ACE2 on the mucous membranes of the oral cavity, especially the tongue, and the dependence of taste perception on smell, with patients with retronasal olfactory dysfunction reporting accompanying gustatory dysfunction
special_populations_notes: Children/adolescents included (age range 12-73 years); age subgroup over 55 years n=15 with no significant differences in olfactory scores; no taste-specific special-population findings
funding_conflicts: Funding: This research received no external funding; Conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Single-visit psychophysical testing (Sniffin' Sticks for smell; Taste Strips mean score 3.53, SD 0.91, range 0-4). Weak non-significant correlations between olfactory and taste scores. Limitation stated: COVID-19 status information obtained mainly from medical interview; subjects did not have test results with them - confirmation coded laboratory-confirmed (assay not stated) per R7(a) on the basis of the stated inclusion criterion of a positive test.

country_setting: India; JSS Hospital, Mysuru (COVID-19 care/sample collection centers)
population_description: COVID-19 patients aged 18-60 years of either sex, RT-PCR positive, selected for dysfunction in both smell and taste, recruited consecutively from COVID-19 sample collection centers; mean age 42 years
taste_types_reported: hypogeusia / unspecified taste dysfunction (reduced ability to taste sweet, salty and bitter more than sour)
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (standardized taste solution/strip test per Gupta et al.: 4 concentrations each of sweet, sour, salty, bitter; score 0-16), plus digital quantification of fungiform papillae
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: participants selected for dysfunction in both smell and taste; Discussion reports 70% reported a loss of smell and 80% had a loss of taste among the 57 participants (as printed)
pathogenesis_finding: Study found a statistically significant positive correlation between taste scores and fungiform papillae density (r = 0.518, P < 0.001); paper notes the ACE2 receptor assisting SARS-CoV-2 invasion is found in taste buds and that an inflammatory response from cytokine release following ACE2 binding has been proposed
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: Financial support and sponsorship - Nil; Conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Cross-sectional taste score (not a change): mean taste score 10 +/- 1.363 (range 7-12) as printed in Table 2; text elsewhere prints inconsistent values (11.7 +/- 1.7). Sex counts inconsistent between text (34 females, 23 males) and Table 3 (Male n=34, Female n=23); copied text version in population field without sex counts. Stated limitation: duration of symptoms could not be investigated.

design: case series >=10 | case series prospective study (paper's wording)
country_setting: Iraq; ENT Department, Martyr Ghazi Al-Hariri Hospital, Baghdad Medical City Complex (outpatient clinic)
population_description: Adults over 18 years with mild or moderate COVID-19 (PCR-positive) and subjective loss of smell persistent for more than one week after symptom onset, recruited from an ENT outpatient clinic and primary care referrals, June 2020-October 2021; mean age 34.3 years
taste_types_reported: unspecified taste dysfunction (loss of taste recorded as a symptom)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (loss of taste recorded at interview; olfaction tested objectively with the Connecticut Chemosensory Clinical Research Center n-butanol test, taste not objectively tested)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING (sample selected for olfactory dysfunction): loss of taste 206/300 (68.7%)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: not reported (recovery duration bands printed for olfactory dysfunction only: up to 1 month 47.7%, 1-2 months 25%, longest band 10-16 months 1.7%; taste persistence not reported separately)
intervention: Smell exercise (self-administered smell training) plus daily supplements: alpha-lipoic acid, omega-3, and zinc (given to all patients until recovery)
intervention_dose_course: Smell exercise: short gentle sniffs of lemon, clove, mint, vanilla, ground pepper and garlic (coffee as neutralizer), 20 seconds per material, repeated 2-3 times per material with 5-minute breaks, twice daily. Supplements: alpha-lipoic acid 600 mg/day, omega III 1 g twice daily, zinc 8 mg/day, until recovery
treatment_recovery_as_printed: Recovery reported for olfactory dysfunction only (not taste-specific): 270/300 (90%) recovered within 16 months; recovered with smell exercise: anosmia 194/208 (64.7% of total cohort as printed), hyposmia 76/92 (25.3% as printed); mean recovery time anosmia 1.61 months, hyposmia 1.88 months; median 1 month each. Taste recovery not reported separately
special_populations_notes: Older adults: occurrence of olfactory dysfunction declined in older age groups (0.7% for anosmia and hyposmia in the over-60 group); patients with severe COVID-19 were excluded
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported; Conflicts: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist
extractor_notes: Study is olfactory-focused; taste captured only as a recorded symptom (loss of taste 68.7%). All patients received smell exercise and supplements, so cohort recovery is recorded under treatment per R3, but it is olfactory recovery, not taste recovery. Mechanisms discussed (neuroepithelial invasion, peripheral/central olfactory mechanisms, nasal obstruction/inflammatory edema) are smell-only - not Q2-coded per R5.

design: case-control | exploratory study of two post-COVID-19 groups with (Group 1) and without (Group 2) chemosensory impairment at disease onset (paper's wording)
country_setting: Italy; University Hospital of Verona
N_total: recruited 44 ; completed 39 (Group 1: 20 ; Group 2: 19) ; healthy pre-pandemic taste controls 37
population_description: Post-COVID-19 patients aged 40-67 years selected by an infectious disease specialist and classified by whether they reported smell/taste impairment at disease onset; assessed several months after onset (median 292 days Group 1, 149 days Group 2); 8 per group had been hospitalized, the rest had mild disease
taste_types_reported: dysgeusia; hypogeusia; ageusia (for single taste qualities)
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (Taste Strips Test, TST, 16 strips, score 0-16; score <9 = hypogeusia)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: dysgeusia present in 18/20 Group 1 vs 0/19 Group 2; hypogeusia (TST <9) in 5/20 Group 1 vs 2/19 Group 2; normogeusia 15/20 Group 1 and 17/19 Group 2; single-quality ageusia only in Group 1 (2 sweet, 3 sour, 1 bitter)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Group 1 assessed at median 292 days (Q1-Q3 246-362) after COVID-19 onset with dysgeusia still present in 18/20 at assessment (>=12wk time point as printed)
pathogenesis_finding: Paper proposes SARS-CoV-2 may impair taste by directly impacting gustatory epithelial cells or the gustatory pathway, or indirectly via inflammatory cytokine storm; ACE2 and TMPRSS2 are expressed in the oral cavity including taste cells, tongue epithelium and salivary glands, and salivary secretory dysfunction might have a role in dysgeusia persistence; this study's MRI found no significant chemosensory correlations after correction, suggesting a more peripheral gustatory system involvement
special_populations_notes: Patients with diabetes were excluded (comorbidity affecting smell/taste performance); authors discuss the perimenopause/menopause age range (50-65 years) as a possible period of female vulnerability to persisting chemosensory deficit
funding_conflicts: Funding: Open access funding provided by Universita degli Studi di Verona within the CRUI-CARE Agreement; MRI costs (COVIDOLFANEURO project) covered by Verona University Hospital research funds (Fondo per la Ricerca Indipendente, FRI); Conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Single cross-sectional assessment months after onset; TST scores (not changes): Group 1 mean 10.6 +/- 3.1, median 11.0; Group 2 mean 11.7 +/- 2.7, median 12.0; Group 1 differed significantly from healthy controls (p = 0.005). Groups sampled by chemosensory-outcome status at onset, hence case-control coding and R2 prefix.

country_setting: Norway; Institute of Clinical Dentistry, University of Oslo (Clinic of Smell, Taste and Oral Pain)
population_description: Post-COVID-19 patients referred from all parts of Norway to a university clinic for persisting smell, taste and trigeminal dysfunction, consecutively recruited October 2020-June 2023 (mean age 41.7 years; 68% female; mostly mild/moderate COVID-19), compared with pre-pandemic healthy controls
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (Taste Strips, Burghart, score 0-16) plus self-reported taste VAS 0-10 and questionnaire for dysgeusia
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING (clinic sample referred for persisting dysfunction): in post-COVID-19 patients - dysgeusia 34.0%, complete ageusia 3.0%, specific ageusia 27.0%, hypogeusia 11.0% (controls: 0.0% for dysgeusia, ageusia and specific ageusia; hypogeusia 15.8%); among patients with specific ageusia, bitter 66.7%, salt 37.0%, sour 33.3%, sweet 3.7%
onset_timing: onset of chemosensory loss about 5 days after the COVID-19 infection in 90.0% of the patients (composite smell/taste as printed)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Patients assessed at mean 12.4 +/- 7.2 months (range 2.0-39.0) after COVID-19 diagnosis with persisting dysfunctions (post-COVID-19 referred sample)
pathogenesis_finding: Paper states ACE2 is expressed in gustatory cells, oral epithelial cells and salivary gland cells, and reduced ACE2 expression due to SARS-CoV-2 infection could be part of the explanation for disturbances in smell, taste and salivary secretory rate; cited work shows human type II taste cells express ACE2 and are infected by SARS-CoV-2
special_populations_notes: Post-COVID-19 patients had significantly more chronic conditions (40.0%) and used more medications (mean 0.8) than controls; no taste-specific special-population findings
funding_conflicts: Funding: external grants from the University of Oslo (Life Science), Robert og Ella Wenzins legat ved Universitetet i Oslo, and Stiftelsen til Tannlegevitenskapens Fremme; Conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Virus confirmation mixed: questionnaire recorded mode of confirmation as PCR test, home test, antibody test or clinical symptoms (per R7e). Cross-sectional VAS taste score (not a change): median 4.5 (IQR 2.0-6.0) in patients vs 8.0 in controls. Phantosmia/phantogeusia were not evaluated (stated). Most common dysfunction combination was olfactory + gustatory (48.0%).

country_setting: Brazil; primary health care (Family Health Care Unit, Joao Pessoa, Paraiba)
population_description: Non-hospitalized adults aged 18 years or older presenting with acute respiratory infection symptoms at a primary care facility between March 1 and December 31, 2021; mean age 41.6 years in the positive group
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (standardized diagnostic screening questionnaire; self-assessment of current taste function)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: In SARS-CoV-2-positive patients: taste disorder only 27/300 (9.0%); both olfactory and taste disorders 105/300 (35.0%); any olfactory/taste disorder 152/300 (50.7%). In SARS-CoV-2-negative patients: taste only 21/463 (4.5%); both 55/463 (11.9%)
pathogenesis_finding: Discussion lists among the most cited mechanisms the interconnection of retronasal olfaction to taste perception and direct damage of taste function caused by the presence of the virus (alongside olfactory-epithelium inflammation/invasion via ACE2)
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: none; Conflicts: the authors declare there is no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Taste and smell reported through grouped olfactory/taste disorder (OTD) categories; taste-specific figures are the 'taste only' and 'both' strata as printed - no combined taste-only-plus-both percentage is printed and none was computed. OTD frequency in positives was higher in females (71.8%) than males (34.3%).

design: retrospective cohort | retrospective medical record review with a prospective follow-up arm (paper's wording: longitudinal study)
country_setting: Singapore; emergency department of Sengkang General Hospital (regional tertiary hospital)
N_total: eligible 56 ; recruited and followed up 40 ; completed objective smell testing (B-SIT) 33
population_description: Singapore citizens and permanent residents aged 21 years and above who presented to the emergency department with COVID-19 between February and May 2020; median age 40 years, male predominance, most with mild COVID-19 (median hospital stay 7 days)
taste_types_reported: unspecified taste dysfunction; ageusia (complete gustatory loss reported by slightly over half of affected subjects)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom (gustatory symptoms documented on a standard proforma at ED presentation; recovery by interviewer-administered phone questionnaire; objective testing performed for smell only, B-SIT)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: self-reported acute gustatory loss at diagnosis 57.5% (olfactory loss 62.5%)
onset_timing: not reported (gustatory symptoms documented upon presentation to the emergency department)
recovery_any_as_printed: 87% of patients with gustatory dysfunction reported that they had recovered by the follow-up phone interview (median 41 weeks from diagnosis)
time_to_recovery_as_printed: all recovery occurred within the first 5 weeks after presentation to the ED
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: follow-up at median 41 weeks after diagnosis (>=12wk): 87% of gustatory dysfunction patients reported recovery; the remainder had not recovered (as printed)
special_populations_notes: none reported
follow_up_duration: 36 weeks (planned follow-up; median time from diagnosis to questionnaire 41 weeks)
funding_conflicts: Funding: This study is fully funded by Sengkang General Hospital; Conflicts: There are no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested for taste dysfunction. During the acute illness, systemic corticosteroids were used in one patient and intranasal corticosteroids in four others (COVID-19 treatment, not taste-directed; numbers too small for analysis) - not entered as a Q3 intervention. Ambidirectional design: cohort and baseline gustatory status ascertained retrospectively from ED records, recovery ascertained prospectively by phone at 36+ weeks. Full text was a scraped journal web page; Tables 1-2 were not readable in the scrape, so figures are those printed in the body text.

design: prospective cohort | case-control study (abstract) / cohort study (methods) - conflicting paper wording
country_setting: Italy; Trieste and Treviso (hospital-recruited cases; hospital staff controls)
N_total: enrolled 100 cases and 100 controls ; analysed 88 cases and 88 matched controls
population_description: Individuals with mild COVID-19 (symptoms without lower respiratory disease, oxygen saturation >=94%) who tested RT-PCR positive in March-April 2020 in Trieste, randomly selected, with age- and sex-matched SARS-CoV-2-negative hospital staff controls; median age 49 years
taste_types_reported: hypogeusia (gustatory dysfunction defined as Taste Strips Score <9)
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (Taste Strips test, Burghart) plus self-reported chemosensory function via SNOT-22 item 'sense of smell or taste' (composite)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Psychophysical gustatory dysfunction (TSS <9) in cases: 26.1% (23/88) at 1 year, 13.6% (12/88) at 2 years, 11.4% (10/88) at 3 years. Self-reported smell or taste dysfunction (composite): 64.8% (57/88) acute phase, 31.8% (28/88) at 1 year, 20.5% (18/88) at 2 years, 15.9% (17/88) at 3 years (as printed)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Gustatory dysfunction (TSS <9) prevalence 26.1% (23/88) at 1 year, 13.6% (12/88) at 2 years and 11.4% (10/88) at 3 years after infection (all >=12wk time points as printed); no significant excess of gustatory dysfunction vs controls at 2 and 3 years
special_populations_notes: Age younger than 50 years was associated with a better Taste Strips Score in both groups; comorbidities recorded (diabetes in 1 case and 1 control; immune suppression in 1 case)
follow_up_duration: 3 years (assessments at median 409, 765 and 1155 days from first positive swab)
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported (obtained funding attributed to Dr Menini, source not stated in text); Conflicts: Dr Hummel reported nonfinancial support from Burghart, personal fees from Primavera and others, and grants from Smell and Taste Lab and Takasago; no other disclosures were reported
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Design conflict flagged per R1(a): abstract calls it a case-control study, methods call it a cohort study; participants were sampled by infection status (exposure) and cases followed prospectively for 3 years, coded prospective cohort. Taste Strips Score values by time point are in Supplement eTable 2, not in the main text, so score change is 'not reported'. Year given as 2023 (published online November 9, 2023; journal issue January 2024).

design: retrospective cohort | retrospective analysis of medical records (paper's wording)
country_setting: Korea; otorhinolaryngology outpatient department, Konkuk University Medical Center, Seoul
N_total: selected 21 C19OD and 66 non-COVID-19 PIOD patients ; analysed 14 C19OD and 55 PIOD (abstract reports 56 PIOD)
virus: SARS-CoV-2 (C19OD group); unspecified postinfectious, non-COVID-19 upper respiratory infection (PIOD group)
population_description: Patients visiting an ENT outpatient clinic with decreased sense of smell after infection: COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction (C19OD, positive PCR March 2020-December 2022; mean age 30.1 years) versus non-COVID-19 postinfectious olfactory dysfunction (PIOD, after upper respiratory infection 2015-2019; mean age 55.7 years); overall age range 10-74 years
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (chemical gustometry: six dilutions of sweet, salty, bitter, sour and umami; detection and recognition scores)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING (sample selected for olfactory dysfunction): taste dysfunction prevalence not reported (gustometry scores only)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: not reported (mean duration of olfactory dysfunction at presentation was 4.75 months in C19OD and 5.52 months in PIOD; taste persistence not reported)
pathogenesis_finding: Paper notes ACE2 is abundantly distributed in epithelial cells of the tongue, basal cells of the nasal cavity and acinar cells of the salivary gland, suggesting a high possibility of chemosensory dysfunction, and assumes olfactory function is most important to gustatory function in C19OD
intervention: Olfactory training
intervention_dose_course: Five odors (lemon, rose, cinnamon, peach, orange) sniffed for 10 seconds each at 10-second intervals, twice a day (morning and evening), for an average of 8 weeks (+/- 4 weeks), with a daily report
N_per_arm: C19OD 14 ; non-COVID-19 PIOD 55 (both groups received olfactory training; groups differ by etiology, not by treatment)
treatment_recovery_as_printed: Recovery outcome reported for olfaction only: KVSS II total score rose from 21.77 +/- 5.48 to 22.64 +/- 5.22 in C19OD (not significant, P = 0.419) and from 17.40 +/- 6.16 to 21.25 +/- 6.45 in non-COVID-19 PIOD (P < 0.001); gustatory function was assessed only at the first visit and was not re-evaluated after training, so taste treatment recovery is not reported
special_populations_notes: Children included (overall age range 10-74 years; C19OD range 10-62); patients with hypothyroidism or liver cirrhosis were excluded
funding_conflicts: Funding: National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Korean government (NRF-2022R1F1A1068186); Conflicts: The authors have no potential conflicts of interest to disclose
extractor_notes: Virus confirmation mixed per R7(e): C19OD confirmed by real-time PCR; PIOD group had no confirmed COVID-19 and post-URTI status was clinical. Baseline chemical gustometry: C19OD had significantly higher detection scores for sweet, salty, sour and umami and higher recognition scores for sweet and salty than PIOD, while bitter scores were higher in PIOD. Internal N inconsistencies as printed (abstract 14/56; methods flow 14/55 analysed of 21/66 selected; demographics table uses 21/66).

design: prospective cohort | longitudinal cohort study (paper's wording)
country_setting: Netherlands; general population (Lifelines biobank, north of the Netherlands)
N_total: responded to at least one questionnaire 235,722 ; Lifelines cohort 167,729 ; invited over 305,500
virus: SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19 positive group) versus non-COVID-19 causes (negative group)
population_description: Adults aged 18 years or older in the Dutch Lifelines population cohort who completed digital COVID-19 questionnaires between March 2020 and May 2022; median age 56 years; grouped by ever versus never having COVID-19
taste_types_reported: unspecified taste dysfunction (composite smell/taste loss only)
taste_measurement: composite smell-taste (single self-report item 'loss of sense of smell or taste' on a 5-point Likert scale, 1 = not at all to 5 = extremely)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported (taste not reported separately from smell; composite: 13,058/235,722 (5.5%) ever reported smell/taste loss; incidence per questionnaire shown only in a figure)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Survival outcome (probability of still having smell or taste loss at the latest measured time point, composite as printed): 0.12 (SE 0.03, 95% CI 0.07-0.21) for COVID-19 related cases and 0.17 (SE 0.03, 95% CI 0.12-0.24) for non-COVID-19 cases; time axis is subsequent questionnaires after onset, not weeks
special_populations_notes: none reported
follow_up_duration: 27 questionnaires from 30 March 2020 to 4 May 2022; duration analyses used the 10 subsequent questionnaires after symptom onset
funding_conflicts: Funding: The Lifelines initiative was made possible by subsidy from the Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport, the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs, the University Medical Center Groningen, Groningen University and the Provinces in the north of the Netherlands; Conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Taste measured only as a composite with smell (single Likert item) - taste_measurement recorded as composite per the form's instruction. Virus confirmation mixed per R7(e): the COVID-19 definition changed over the study period (doctor's diagnosis; PCR test in a healthcare facility; later positive self-administered home test or PCR at any organization). COVID-19 related loss was more severe but shorter in duration than non-COVID-19 loss.

design: prospective cohort | prospective observational study (paper's wording; pooled analysis of two cohorts)
country_setting: Italy; Trieste University Hospital and Treviso General Hospital (home-managed patients)
N_total: baseline 517 (Trieste 315 ; Treviso 202) ; completed all follow-up interviews 437 ; analysed 403
population_description: Adults aged 18 years or older with mildly symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection (PCR positive 1-22 March 2020) considered suitable for home management, consecutively assessed at two hospitals in Northeast Italy; median age 52 years, 56.9% women
taste_types_reported: unspecified taste dysfunction (composite smell or taste alteration only)
taste_measurement: composite smell-taste (SNOT-22 item 'sense of smell or taste', graded 0-5, by structured telephone questionnaire)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported (taste not reported separately from smell; composite altered sense of smell or taste: 267/403 (66.3%) at baseline, 56 (13.9%) at 6-12 months, 29 (7.2%) at 2 years, 21 (5.2%) at 3 years)
recovery_complete_as_printed: Among the 267 patients with smell or taste dysfunction at baseline (composite): complete resolution 79.0% at 6-12 months (211/267), 89.1% at 2 years, 92.1% (246/267) at 3 years
recovery_any_as_printed: Of patients still experiencing dysfunction 2 years after COVID-19, 27.6% recovered completely and 37.9% recovered partially (improved) at the 3-year follow-up (composite as printed)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Altered sense of smell or taste (composite) persisted in 56/403 (13.9%) at 6-12 months, 29/403 (7.2%) at 2 years and 21/403 (5.2%) at 3 years; discussion states 7.9% of those with an acute-phase alteration still reported symptoms 3 years after COVID-19
special_populations_notes: none reported
follow_up_duration: 3 years (evaluations at median 4, 298, 724 and 1092 days from first positive swab)
funding_conflicts: Funding: None; Conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested (olfactory training mentioned in discussion as the most effective existing strategy but not tested in this study). Taste measured only as a composite with smell via a single SNOT-22 item. Duplicate-cohort suspicion: Trieste series overlaps with the same group's psychophysical cohort studies from March-April 2020 (see also R00457 in this review, a separate matched psychophysical study). UGT2A1/UGT2A2 sustentacular-cell mechanism discussed is olfactory - not taste-extended, not Q2-coded per R5.

design: cross-sectional | online survey (largest taste dataset) with an additional prospective observational cohort (CovILD)
country_setting: Austria and Italy (Tyrol and South Tyrol); online survey of ambulatory patients plus hospital cohort in Austria
N_total: survey respondents 3,140 ; survey analysed 906 (Austria 479 ; Italy 427) ; CovILD observational cohort analysed 108
population_description: Survey: adult ambulatory non-hospitalized COVID-19 convalescents with symptomatic infection and at least 90 days between diagnosis and survey (median age 43-45 years, 67-70% female). CovILD cohort: COVID-19 outpatients and inpatients (mild 25%, moderate 51%, severe/ICU 24%), median age 56 years
taste_measurement: self-report symptom (survey symptom-duration categories; cohort symptom recording at follow-up visits; taste not objectively tested)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Survey study, acute COVID-19: self-reported taste disorders in 68% (Austria) and 74% (Italy) of participants; at 90 days after onset: 22% (Austria) and 21% (Italy). CovILD cohort: taste prevalence not reported (olfactory dysfunction only)
onset_timing: taste disorders present during acute COVID-19 (first 14 days after clinical onset) as printed
time_to_recovery_as_printed: median recovery time for self-reported taste disorders was 14 days (survey study); the persistent smell and taste disorder cluster had a median recovery of 90 days (composite, as printed in the abstract)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: taste disorders still present 90 days after COVID-19 onset in 22% (Austria) and 21% (Italy) of survey convalescents (>=12wk time point as printed)
pathogenesis_finding: Authors state the co-occurrence of subjective olfactory dysfunction and taste disorders (in >66% of convalescents at 3 months) is likely a result of impaired retronasal smell
special_populations_notes: CovILD cohort had high comorbidity burden (75% with comorbidities, including type 2 diabetes 15% and immune deficiency 5.6%); the persistent smell and taste disorder survey cluster was predominantly young, female and comorbidity-free
follow_up_duration: 360 days (CovILD cohort); survey analysis required at least 90 days since diagnosis (median observation 140-180 days)
funding_conflicts: Funding: grants of Land Tirol (GZ 71934) and Boehringer Ingelheim (IIS 1199-0424); open access funding provided by University of Innsbruck and Medical University of Innsbruck; Conflicts: no support from any organization for the submitted work; one author (PT) owns a data science enterprise and received an honorarium for statistical analysis and scientific writing; no other relationships declared
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested (olfactory training mentioned as potentially accelerating OD recovery, not tested). Multi-design paper coded by the largest taste dataset (survey) per R1(e); taste data come only from the survey study - the CovILD cohort reported olfactory outcomes (objective Sniffin' Sticks testing was smell only).

design: other (retrospective Twitter infodemiology study - unit of analysis is tweets, not patients)
country_setting: France; Twitter (French-language tweets)
N_total: extracted 307,290 French tweets (Jan-Mar 2020) ; taste-related keyword tweets 237,999 ; ageusia-keyword tweets 12,544 ; manually annotated ageusia-related tweets 400
population_description: French Twitter users posting tweets containing anosmia- or ageusia-related keywords between January 1 and March 31, 2020 (public social-media posts, not a recruited patient cohort)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom (symptom mentions in tweets detected by fuzzy matching against a MedDRA-based dictionary, with manual annotation of random samples)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported (no patient denominator; of 400 manually annotated ageusia-related tweets, 59 (14.8%) contained genuine ageusia symptoms, of which 43 reported experienced loss of taste and 25/59 (42.4%) were COVID-19-related, all after March 10, 2020)
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: The authors received no specific funding for this study; Conflicts: MT, PF, AM and SS are members of Kap Code, a start-up that owns the Detec't extraction tool
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Infodemiology study: no patients were examined and no COVID-19 status was verified; tweet-level proportions are not patient prevalence and are flagged as such in the prevalence field. First two authors (Faviez and Talmatkadi) contributed equally; first author taken as Faviez per the author-contributions statement.

design: case series >=10 | non-concurrent multiple baseline across participants single-case design (proof-of-concept study)
country_setting: United Kingdom (London laboratory; participants residing in different parts of the UK)
population_description: Adults aged 20-62 years (5 males, 10 females) with persistent (>10 days) smell and/or taste impairment following COVID-19, recruited via social media and charities; mean duration of impairment before intervention 236.66 days (range 28-817)
taste_measurement: psychophysical test (ODOFIN Taste Strips, 4-strip identification test) ; self-report questionnaire (7-point severity ratings 0-6 for loss of taste and distorted taste)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: enrolment required persistent smell and/or taste impairment after COVID-19; 13 of the 15 participants had taste impairment at pre-intervention assessment
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: cohort selected for persistent impairment: mean duration 236.66 days (range 28-817) before intervention; 10 participants had impairment for more than 24 weeks (Table 3)
taste_score_change_as_printed: Subjective loss-of-taste rating 3.20 (SD 1.97) pre-CVFLA vs 1.00 (SD 1.07) post (p<0.001); distorted taste 3.13 (1.99) vs 1.40 (1.30) (p=0.004); ODOFIN taste test total 3.12 (0.99) vs 3.87 (0.35) (p=0.08, n=8 with paired objective data)
intervention: Camera-Based Visual Feedback Learning Aid (CVFLA): camera-based visual feedback training with a collar obscuring the direct view of the self while participants smell/taste food items (apparatus patent no. 10186160)
intervention_dose_course: Up to 10 sessions over 5-10 weeks, each up to 60 minutes (mean 7.47 sessions, SD 2.56; mean total duration 389.96 min, SD 150.93), preceded by 7-, 14- or 21-day baseline symptom monitoring
comparator: none (uncontrolled; each participant acted as own control across staggered baselines)
N_per_arm: 7-day baseline n=5 ; 14-day baseline n=4 ; 21-day baseline n=6
treatment_recovery_as_printed: No complete-recovery proportion for taste printed; 11 of 13 participants with taste impairment showed a reduction in severity of taste impairment post-intervention, and 11 of 13 showed a less distorted sense of taste; all 15 participants showed some reduction in total (smell and taste) impairment on subjective ratings
adverse_events_as_printed: not reported; no drop-outs due to the intervention; one participant reported concerns regarding body image issues once they began to enjoy food after the fourth CVFLA session
special_populations_notes: Adults only (age >=18 required); one participant had rhinitis and one had asthma; no neurodegenerative disorders
follow_up_duration: Post-intervention assessment 1 week after the last intervention session
funding_conflicts: Funding: Brunel University London, the European Research Development Fund (EDRF) and Learning JBE Ltd via Anglia Ruskin University; Conflict of interest: JB was employed by Learning JBE Ltd; the remaining authors declare no conflicts
extractor_notes: Single-arm proof-of-concept intervention study; improvement is reported as severity-score change, not as recovery, so score changes are in the score-change field and no recovery proportion was derived. No viral pathogenesis mechanism for taste loss is proposed (the intervention rationale is central visual-feedback relearning), so Q2 fields are blank.

country_setting: not reported
population_description: Six patients (ages 20-57 years) with persistent olfactory and gustatory dysfunction after recovering from COVID-19, with symptom durations from 5 months to more than 1.5 years
taste_measurement: self-report questionnaire/interview (patient self-reported percentage improvement; no psychophysical testing performed)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: all 6 patients were selected because they had persistent anosmia, parosmia, ageusia and dysgeusia after COVID-19
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: All 6 patients had long-term dysfunction at presentation (5 months in Case 1; dysgeusia for over 1.5 years in Case 4; anosmia and ageusia for 1.5 years in Cases 5 and 6)
taste_score_change_as_printed: Self-reported taste improvement per case: Case 1, 80% improvement in taste after right SGB; Case 2, 90% improvement after right SGB and complete return of taste after left SGB; Case 3, taste improvement 15% after right SGB, 30% after left SGB, 50% at 1-month and 80% at 3-month follow-up; Case 5, no improvement
pathogenesis_finding: It is hypothesized that these symptoms could be due to the bilateral cervical sympathetic chain being affected during these viral infections, and that dysautonomia could play an important role in the pathophysiology of long COVID, perpetuating a proinflammatory state; impaired cerebral blood flow in dysautonomia can affect the areas of the brain that mediate these sensory functions, and SGB is hypothesised to increase cerebral blood flow, improving perfusion of the cortical areas and peripheral receptors responsible for taste and smell
intervention: Ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block (SGB), right side at the initial visit followed by left side at a subsequent visit
intervention_dose_course: 7 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine or ropivacaine per block (after skin infiltration with 3 mL of 1% lidocaine); one block per side
treatment_recovery_as_printed: All but one patient reported improvements in olfaction and gustation after the SGB; five out of six patients demonstrated varying degrees of taste and smell perception improvement; 83% of the patients experienced significant improvements in their symptoms; Case 2 reported a complete return of taste after the second (left-sided) SGB; Case 5 reported no improvement at the three-week follow-up
adverse_events_as_printed: Side effects and complications observed in the series include temporary ptosis, conjunctival erythema, dysphonia, dysphagia, and hypopharyngeal anesthesia; the symptoms were transient and well-tolerated
special_populations_notes: none reported (individual comorbidities included pre-diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, migraine headaches, dyslipidemia, hypertension and depression)
follow_up_duration: Telephone follow-up the day after each procedure; additional follow-up between one month and four months following the second SGB, varying by patient
funding_conflicts: All authors declared that no financial support was received from any organization for the submitted work and that they have no financial relationships or other relationships/activities that could appear to have influenced the work
extractor_notes: Case series of 6 patients (below the >=10 threshold for the form's case-series category). All outcomes are patient self-reported percentage improvements; no objective gustatory testing was performed, as the authors acknowledge. COVID-19 confirmation method is not stated for any case.

country_setting: Spain (five urban public hospitals in Madrid)
N_total: 7150 hospitalized during the first wave ; 2000 randomly selected ; 1969 included at T0/T1 ; 1593 evaluated at T2 ; 1266 completed all follow-ups (final analysis sample)
population_description: Previously hospitalized COVID-19 survivors from the first pandemic wave (10 March-31 May 2020); final sample 46.5% women, mean age 61 years (SD 16)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom (telephone interview; ageusia defined as a self-perceived feeling of complete loss of taste attributed to the infection)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Ageusia 7.10% (n=89) at infection onset/hospitalization (T0), 3.03% (n=38) at T1 (mean 8.4 months), 1.99% (n=25) at T2 (mean 13.2 months) and 1.36% (n=17) at T3 (mean 18.3 months) after hospital discharge
recovery_complete_as_printed: 87.6% (n=78/89) of those experiencing ageusia at the onset of COVID-19 (T0) had recovered at T1 (about 8.4 months)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Ageusia still present in 1.36% (n=17) at T3 (mean 18.3 months after discharge); only 11 patients (0.88%) self-reported ageusia throughout all follow-up periods
special_populations_notes: Older hospitalized cohort (mean age 61 years); no variable was associated with the development of ageusia at any post-COVID follow-up
follow_up_duration: Telephone follow-ups at mean 8.4 (T1), 13.2 (T2) and 18.3 (T3) months after hospital discharge
funding_conflicts: Funding: Fondo Europeo de Desarrollo Regional - Recursos REACT-UE del Programa Operativo de Madrid 2014-2020 (LONG-COVID-EXP-CM); Conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Ageusia measured only as complete loss of taste by self-report at each wave; prevalence denominators are the 1266 participants completing all follow-ups. No taste-specific pathogenesis mechanism is proposed, so Q2 fields are blank.

country_setting: Saudi Arabia (web-based survey of residents, distributed via social media)
N_total: 1461 completed the questionnaire ; 922 with a history of SARS-CoV-2 infection included in the analysis
population_description: Saudi and non-Saudi adults aged 18 years or older residing in Saudi Arabia with a self-reported history of SARS-CoV-2 infection (561 males, 361 females; 54.3% aged 18-29 years); convenience sample recruited August 2022-January 2023
taste_measurement: self-report questionnaire (self-administered bilingual web questionnaire: taste completely lost / decreased / abnormally changed / not affected)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Ageusia (complete loss of taste) 180 (19.52%), hypogeusia 47 (5.1%), dysgeusia 293 (31.8%); any taste-related disorder 520 (56.39%); taste not affected in 402 (43.6%)
time_to_recovery_as_printed: Self-reported time for sense of taste to recover (percentages of all 922 participants, Table 3): less than 1 month 478 (51.8%), 2-6 months 72 (7.8%), more than 6 months 21 (2.3%), not recovered 33 (3.6%)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: 21 participants (2.3%) took more than 6 months for taste to recover and 33 (3.6%) reported taste not recovered (bands as printed, percentages of all 922 participants)
special_populations_notes: Adults only (age >=18); taste disorders were significantly more common in females (p<0.001) and varied by age group and vaccination status
funding_conflicts: Funding: King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia (project RSP 2023 R47); Conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Internal inconsistency flagged: in Table 5 the ageusia and hypogeusia columns appear transposed relative to Table 3 and the abstract (gender rows sum to 47 for the column labelled ageusia and 180 for hypogeusia, whereas Table 3/abstract report 180 completely lost and 47 decreased); the headline figures follow Table 3/abstract as printed. The ACE2 mechanism discussed concerns the olfactory epithelium and smell only, and the ABO discussion concerns infection susceptibility, so no taste-specific mechanism is Q2-coded per the form's R5.

country_setting: Italy (Friuli Venezia Giulia and Sardinia; university hospitals and tertiary referral centres)
N_total: 482 potentially eligible ; 338 completed the baseline survey ; 294 (87.0%) responded to the 6-month follow-up
population_description: Adults (age >=18) with mild-to-moderate PCR-confirmed COVID-19 managed in home isolation, infected from 17 January 2022 during Omicron BA.1 predominance; follow-up sample median age 46 years (range 21-83), 55.4% women; 83.0% fully vaccinated
taste_types_reported: dysgeusia (altered sense of taste; taste types not further separated)
taste_measurement: self-report questionnaire (SNOT-22 single composite item 'sense of smell or taste', scored 0-5, plus a binary yes/no question on whether the dysfunction involved smell, taste, or both; taste not measured separately from smell in the severity item)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Altered sense of smell or taste (composite) 101/294 (34.4%) in the acute phase and 4/294 (1.4%) at 6 months; by type at baseline: smell and taste 67 (22.8%), only taste 18 (6.1%), only smell 16 (5.4%); at 6 months: smell and taste 3 (1.0%), only taste 0 (0.0%), only smell 1 (0.3%)
recovery_complete_as_printed: Among the 101 patients with COVID-19-associated smell or taste dysfunction during the acute phase, 97 (96.0%) reported complete resolution at 6 months (composite smell-or-taste outcome)
recovery_any_as_printed: Of the 101 patients with acute-phase dysfunction, 2 (2.0%) reported a decrease in severity and 2 (2.0%) reported the symptom worse at 6 months (composite)
time_to_recovery_as_printed: Median duration of chemosensory impairment (composite) 6 days in fully vaccinated vs 8 days in non/partially vaccinated patients (p=0.007); median 4 days for isolated smell or taste dysfunction vs 7 days when both senses were affected (p=0.045)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Altered sense of smell or taste persisted in 4/294 (1.4%) at 6 months, including smell and taste involvement in 3 (1.0%) and only taste in 0 (0.0%)
pathogenesis_finding: It is well known that patients may self-report loss of taste when they develop loss of flavor perception because of an impairment in the retronasal olfactory function; thus, some patients with isolated alteration of the sense of smell may have suffered less extensive damage to the olfactory neuroepithelium such as not to compromise the retronasal sense of smell and characterized by faster recovery times
special_populations_notes: Adults only; patients with pre-existing self-reported smell and taste dysfunction, prior oral/nasal surgery or radiotherapy, head trauma, allergic rhinitis or chronic rhinosinusitis were excluded
funding_conflicts: Funding: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article; Declaration of competing interest: The authors declare that there is no conflict of interest
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested (vaccination status is an observational exposure, not a tested intervention). Taste severity was measured only within the composite SNOT-22 'sense of smell or taste' item; taste-specific data are limited to the yes/no type breakdown copied into the prevalence field. The TMPRSS2/syncytia and mucosal IgA mechanisms discussed concern olfactory dysfunction and are not Q2-coded per R5.

country_setting: Egypt (Assiut University hospitals)
population_description: Children and adults with persistent post-COVID-19 smell disorders (with or without taste disorders) lasting >=6 months, evaluated at a university hospital; adults mean age 31.41 years (SD 8.63), children mean age 15.66 years (SD 1.63); 96 females (51.9%) and 89 males (48.1%)
taste_measurement: psychophysical test (Sniffin' taste and flavor identification tests) ; self-report questionnaire (clinical questionnaire for smell and taste; taste disorder defined as subjective loss or distortion of all or any of the 5 basic tastes)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: patients were enrolled with persistent smell disorders (with or without taste disorders) for >=6 months; on objective testing, ageusia and flavor loss were found in 20% (n=37) of the 185 patients; subjectively, taste and flavor losses were the complaint of 79.46% (n=147) at presentation
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Whole cohort selected for disorders persisting >=6 months; duration of disorders at assessment 11.53 ± 3.97 months (range 6-24 months)
pathogenesis_finding: Evidence from experimental studies suggested that injury and degeneration of the neuronal olfactory and gustatory sensory epithelia by severe peripheral viral infection and its immunopathology and the delay or lack of neuronal regeneration might contribute to these disorders; the occurrence of taste, flavor and trigeminal sensory losses at lower frequencies and differential taste loss in some patients support that viral infection could involve taste and trigeminal tissues independent to smell
intervention: Treatments received by patients before/during care (not assigned by the study): nasal irrigations, local steroids, systemic steroids, and vitamins and supplements (zinc, omega-3, vitamin B complex, vitamins C and E, selenium, L-carnitine, pentoxifylline); 42 patients also self-practised sniffing strong odors (essential oils/scents) or pungent herbs
intervention_dose_course: Nasal irrigations 3-15 days (mean 8.34 ± 3.86); local steroids 6-60 days (mean 18.28 ± 9.94); systemic steroids 3-30 days (mean 11.89 ± 6.41); vitamins/supplements 6-90 days (mean 41.65 ± 24.04); odor sniffing 30-120 days (mean 65.50 ± 32.84)
N_per_arm: 146 (78.92%) received treatment modalities ; 39 (21.08%) had no otolaryngology consultation or treatment
treatment_recovery_as_printed: Patients received different treatment modalities for months, but none was effective; the self-practised odor sniffing also provided no beneficial effect (no per-treatment recovery rates printed)
special_populations_notes: Children included: 35 children/adolescents (mean age 15.66 years) alongside 150 adults; no specific differences in demographics or clinical variables distinguished children from adults
follow_up_duration: not reported (single cross-sectional assessment; disorders had lasted 6-24 months)
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported; Conflict-of-interest statement: All the authors report no relevant conflicts of interest for this article
extractor_notes: Confirmation routes were mixed: only 43 patients (23.24%) had RT-PCR, while investigations included serology and complete blood count (70.3%, n=130) and chest CT (17.3%, n=32). Intervention fields record pre-study treatments reported retrospectively by patients, not a tested intervention; the paper's only outcome statement for them is that none was effective.

country_setting: Bahrain (national COVID-19 registry)
population_description: Adults aged 18 years or more diagnosed with COVID-19 between 1 October 2020 and 30 June 2021, randomly selected from the national COVID-19 registry in Bahrain; mean age 38.2 years (SD 11.3); 220 males (54.3%) and 185 females (45.8%); patients with pre-existing olfactory or taste dysfunction were excluded
taste_measurement: self-report questionnaire (telephone interviews using the AAO-HNS Anosmia Reporting Tool, with the anosmia/dysgeusia question separated, plus the brief Questionnaire of Olfactory Disorders)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Changes in the sense of taste (dysgeusia) reported by 195/405 patients (48.1%); higher in females (102/180, 56.7%) than males (89/217, 41.0%)
pathogenesis_finding: Single cell RNA-sequencing studies showed that epithelial cells of the tongue express ACE-2 receptors where buccal mucosa may play a role in entry of SARS-CoV-2; additionally, indirect damage of the taste receptors through infection and inflammation of the epithelial cells is hypothesised to play a role in the pathogenesis of taste disorders in COVID-19
special_populations_notes: Adults only (age >=18); sex was the only significant predictor of dysgeusia (p=0.001 in the regression model)
funding_conflicts: Funding: The authors have not declared a specific grant for this research from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors; Disclosure: The authors declare that they have no competing interests in this work
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. Although the questionnaire covered onset, duration and resolution, no duration or recovery results for this cohort are reported (the statement that taste/smell loss is mostly transient, lasting one to two weeks, is attributed to prior literature). The ACE2/TMPRSS2 mechanism described for anosmia (olfactory epithelium) is smell-specific and is not Q2-coded per R5.

design: other (bibliographic/narrative review - no primary patient data)
country_setting: not reported (worldwide literature)
N_total: 64 studies on persistent gustatory sequelae with a total of 23,476 COVID-19 survivors ; 86 studies on acute gustatory dysfunction with a total of 42,759 COVID-19 patients (literature totals as printed)
population_description: COVID-19 survivors in published follow-up studies retrieved from PubMed/Medline, LitCovid, ProQuest, medRxiv and bioRxiv (search cutoff 30 September 2022); the review excluded studies whose participants had not been diagnosed by RT-PCR and/or serological test
taste_measurement: not reported (assessment methods varied across the cited primary studies)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Gustatory dysfunction (ageusia, dysgeusia and/or hypogeusia collectively) persists with a prevalence of 1-45% in COVID-19 survivors followed for 21-365 days; summarising 29 follow-up studies, gustatory dysfunction was reported by 13.6% of survivors at 29.7-day follow-up, 13.8% at 60.4-day follow-up and 12.7% at 181.9-day follow-up; ageusia continues in 14.1% of survivors at a mean 67-day follow-up (8 observational studies analysed by Moraschini et al.)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Gustatory dysfunction reported by 12.7% of COVID-19 survivors at a mean follow-up of 181.9 days (29-study summary); across studies, follow-ups ranged from 21 to 365 days with prevalence 1-45%
pathogenesis_finding: ACE2, Furin and TMPRSS2 are abundantly present in taste receptor cell-containing taste buds and taste bud-locating papillae and in ductal, acinar and myoepithelial cells of salivary glands, and viral particles consistent with Coronaviridae were found in salivary gland ductal and acinar cells of fatal COVID-19 cases; taste buds and salivary glands expressing ACE2 are attacked by SARS-CoV-2 and receive collateral damage, adversely affecting taste perception and salivary secretion. In addition, SARS-CoV-2 infection-induced zinc deficiency is proposed: zinc is essential for taste bud physiology and taste cell regeneration, deficiency decreases the number and size of taste buds and taste sensitivity, and serum zinc concentrations are significantly decreased in COVID-19 patients with hypozincemia persisting after recovery
special_populations_notes: none reported (prevalence of gustatory sequelae noted to vary partly with ethnicity, gender, age and disease severity across studies)
follow_up_duration: Follow-ups in the cited studies ranged from 21 to 365 days after infection
funding_conflicts: Funding: JSPS KAKENHI Grant No. 20K10152; Conflict of Interest Statement: The author has no conflicts of interest to declare
extractor_notes: Q3-tagged, no intervention tested. This record is a narrative bibliographic review, not a primary study; all prevalence figures are ranges/summaries of the cited literature as printed in the review, not new patient data. A TRPV1 interaction mechanism for oral tissues is also discussed but rests mainly on rat expression data and is not separately coded.

country_setting: United States (Indiana University Health COVID registry, Indiana)
N_total: survey distributed to 13,561 volunteers ; 225 respondents ; long COVID cohort 127 (121 analysed after excluding hospitalized patients) ; COVID reinfection cohort 47 (43 analysed)
population_description: Adults aged 18 years or older from a COVID-19 research registry who self-identified as having tested positive for COVID-19: a long COVID cohort (single positive test, >=60 days before the survey) and a COVID reinfection cohort (two or more positive tests); mean age 45.8 years (range 19-84); 157 females and 57 males among the 225 respondents; all participants were vaccinated
taste_measurement: self-report questionnaire (electronic REDCap survey; taste perception rated on a 4-point scale: same as before, worse than before, better than before, total loss, compared with pre-COVID)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Taste perception worse than pre-COVID reported by 29% (35/121) of the long COVID cohort and 42% (18/43) of the COVID reinfection cohort; total loss of taste reported by 1 individual in the long COVID cohort and 2 in the reinfection cohort
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Among those with worse taste perception, duration was 12-24 months in 11 (31%) and >24 months in 7 (20%) in the long COVID cohort, and 12-24 months in 12 (67%) and >24 months in 1 (6%) in the reinfection cohort (Table 3); durations overall ranged from 2 to 30 months (long COVID) and 79 to 875 days (reinfection)

country_setting: United States (single outpatient pain clinic; Texas Christian University IRB)
population_description: Patients presenting to a single clinic between February and July 2022 with post-COVID symptomology including parosmia and/or dysgeusia, who underwent stellate ganglion blockade; 157 females (80.5%) and 38 males (19.5%); mean age 38.58 years

funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported; Disclosure: The authors report no conflicts of interest in this work

country_setting: Egypt (Oral and Maxillofacial Department, Faculty of Dentistry, Fayoum University)

recovery_any_as_printed: not reported (recovery reported per treatment arm - see treatment_recovery)

pathogenesis_finding: The pathogenicity of SARS-CoV-2 is initiated by the virus targeting ACE-2 receptors, which allow viral entry into cells; ACE-2 receptors are found throughout the oral mucosa, particularly on the tongue and in the salivary glands; with viral-induced hyperinflammation, downregulation of ACE-2 receptors may result in endothelial dysfunction and dysfunction at viral entry points, revealing a possible mechanism for loss of taste through the interactions between thrombosis and inflammation

special_populations_notes: Adults only; associated olfactory dysfunction reported by 6/18 in Group I and 9/18 in Group II
follow_up_duration: Taste assessed at diagnosis (pre-treatment) and at 1, 2, 3 and 4 weeks post-treatment
funding_conflicts: Funding: open access funding provided by The Science, Technology & Innovation Funding Authority (STDF) in cooperation with The Egyptian Knowledge Bank (EKB); no study grant declared; Competing interests: The authors have no competing interests to declare

N_total: parent cohort (COVID-PSL) 429; with olfactory/gustatory dysfunction 300; enrolled in CIRANO substudy 98

onset_timing: Median delay from first COVID-19 symptoms to gustatory disorders 3 days (IQR 0-4); olfactory/gustatory dysfunction present at onset of COVID-19 in 30%

pathogenesis_finding: Anosmia and ageusia in COVID-19 judged 'very likely to be caused by the involvement of the olfactory and gustatory nervous systems' (neurotropic characteristics of SARS-CoV-2; ACE2-mediated entry into neurons)

country_setting: UK and Italy; two hospitals (London and Padua)
N_total: received questionnaire 155 (London 119; Padua 36); completed initial survey 114; analysed (ongoing taste dysfunction) 47 (London 23; Padua 24)

special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported; Conflicts: authors declare no conflict of interest

design: registry record | retrospective cohort (HOPE COVID-19 Registry subanalysis)

Pathogenesis discussion concerns olfactory epithelium invasion/neuroinvasion and immune activation as a prognostic marker; no taste-specific mechanism proposed - general/olfactory mechanism not taste-extended - not Q2-coded. Record is the registry subanalysis (preprint posted 2 Feb 2021; version of record in Infection, 2021).

country_setting: UK; London community cohort (recruited via primary care text-message invitation)

taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (online questionnaire)

funding_conflicts: Funding: National Institute for Health Research (BRC751; also NIHR grant RP-2015-06-005 and Sir Jules Thorn Trust Biomedical Research Award for some authors); Competing interests: none declared

Participants whose smell/taste loss had lasted >1 month at enrolment were excluded. Objective testing (UPSIT) was of smell only, in a subsample of 50.

country_setting: USA; University of Pennsylvania (tertiary academic medical centre), Philadelphia
N_total: screening responses 302; excluded 22; analysed 250; meeting criteria for smell/taste testing 128
population_description: Adult healthcare workers; mean age 40.3 years (range 18-72); 80.8% female; evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection in 11/250 (4.4%)
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test (self-administered Waterless Empirical Taste Test, SA-WETT, 27 strips; plus self-report survey)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Self-reported dysgeusia in 27/250 (10.8%); recent-onset olfactory and/or gustatory dysfunction in 73% (8/11) of subjects with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection (composite)

pathogenesis_finding: Authors conclude damage to the olfactory system is a primary contributor to reports of taste loss (loss of flavour sensations secondary to olfactory system damage), since objective gustatory scores were normal despite subjective taste loss; ACE2 is expressed in taste buds and an inflammatory process involving cytokine release following ACE2 receptor binding has also been proposed
special_populations_notes: Pregnancy: currently pregnant respondents were excluded from the smell/taste testing
funding_conflicts: Financial disclosures: none; Conflicts: R.L. Doty is a consultant to Eisai Co Ltd, Merck Pharmaceuticals, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research, Septodont Inc and Johnson & Johnson (as printed)
