country_setting: Canada; COVID-19 Assessment Centre, St. Michael's Hospital, Toronto, Ontario (ambulatory)
N_total: identified 1,345 (102 positive ; 1,243 negative) ; contacted 408 (102 positive ; 306 randomly sampled negative) ; completed survey 128 (56 positive ; 72 negative)
population_description: Adults (over 18 years) who underwent COVID-19 testing at an ambulatory assessment centre between 16 March and 15 April 2020; survey respondents: median age 38.0 years (positive) vs 43.0 years (negative)
taste_types_reported: dysgeusia; ageusia (reported as a combined dysgeusia/ageusia category)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (secure online survey after notification of swab result; taste-loss components sweet, salty, sour, bitter, savoury collected)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: dysgeusia/ageusia around the time of COVID-19 symptom onset (5 days before or any time after): 46.4% of positive patients vs 5.6% of negative patients (p<0.001); as an overall symptom: 57.1% of positives vs 1.4% of negatives; concomitant smell and taste loss in 20 (35.7%) positive patients; adjusted OR for dysgeusia/ageusia and COVID-19 positivity 11.4 (95% CI 3.6–45.3)
onset_timing: taste loss was ascertained around the time of COVID-19-like symptom onset (5 days before or any time after); finer timing categories are reported for smell loss only
pathogenesis_finding: "Dysgeusia/ageusia is generally regarded to be secondary to loss of smell, as it may be difficult to distinguish between flavor and taste... the rate of taste loss in our patients likely represents subtle olfactory deficits" (a distinct taste mechanism is noted as possible, citing Vaira et al.)
special_populations_notes: children: only adults (over 18 years) included; diabetes: diabetes in 7.1% of positive and 7.0% of negative respondents
funding_conflicts: Funding: The Dunin Foundation; conflicts: JML has received honoraria from Baxter Corporation; all other authors declared no potential conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Table 1 totals (n=127; negative n=71) differ by one from the text/abstract (56 positive and 72 negative completions); text values extracted. Current ability to smell at survey is reported (52% of those with smell loss normal) but no taste recovery data are printed. No intervention tested.

country_setting: United Kingdom; London — a 430-bed acute teaching hospital (Chelsea and Westminster) and surrounding community testing population
N_total: diagnosed SARS-CoV-2-positive 386 ; included in analysis 141 (92 community ; 49 discharged inpatients) ; non-tested household contacts described separately 185
population_description: Adults (>=16 years) with laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 managed in the community or admitted and discharged from hospital between 1 March and 1 April 2020; mean age 45.6 years (range 20–93); patients who died, current inpatients and those without an accurate symptom history excluded
taste_types_reported: ageusia (defined by the paper as total or partial loss of taste)
taste_measurement: patient-reported scale (symptoms from routinely collected clinical records plus standardised follow-up telephone consultation questions on change in smell and taste)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: ageusia 89/141 (63.1%) overall (community 57/92 (62.0%); admitted 32/49 (65.3%)); anosmia and ageusia together 77/141 (55%); ageusia only in 9 patients; anosmia only in 3 patients
onset_timing: not reported for taste (median onset of anosmia relative to COVID-19 symptom onset was 4 days (IQR 5))
pathogenesis_finding: "Patients who reported ageusia only could not accurately differentiate between losing their sense of taste or their sense of smell. This may be due to retronasal olfactory function being labelled as taste... we therefore made the assumption that ageusia was unlikely to be present in the absence of anosmia"
special_populations_notes: children: patients under 16 years of age excluded
funding_conflicts: Funding: "This research did not receive any grant from funding agencies in the public or commercial sectors"; conflicts: EC received speaker fees from bioMerieux (2019); NM speaker fees from Beyer (2016) and Pfizer (2019) and educational support from Eumedica and Baxter; LSPM consulted for bioMerieux, DNAelectronics, Dairy Crest and Umovis Lab and received speaker fees, research grants (NIHR, CW+ Charity, Leo Pharma) and educational support; AP, DLA and AA declared no conflicts
extractor_notes: Resolution/duration data are reported for anosmia only (49 resolved, 32 unresolved/ongoing hyposmia; median duration 8 days (IQR 16)) — no taste-specific recovery data printed. Household contacts (n=185) were not tested; their data concern anosmia only and are not extracted as taste data. No intervention tested.

country_setting: Italy; three non-intensive care wards in Florence (Internal Medicine and Infectious Disease Units of Santa Maria Annunziata and Nuovo San Giovanni Di Dio hospitals)
population_description: The first 100 adults hospitalized for COVID-19 in non-intensive care wards and discharged a month earlier; all Caucasian; mean age 65 ± 15 years (range 29–94); 60% male; patients with cognitive impairment excluded from follow-up
taste_types_reported: ageusia; dysgeusia (reported together as gustatory dysfunction, GD)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (telephone interview on any alteration/reduction of taste since illness onset; persisting dysfunction scored on a 100-point recovery scale — complete recovery 100 points, near complete 80–95 points)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: gustatory dysfunction (GD) in 41/100 patients (41%); olfactory dysfunction in 29; both GD and OD in 28; any chemosensory dysfunction in 42 patients
onset_timing: all symptomatic patients reported symptoms starting very early, at the most within one week of the first noted symptoms
recovery_complete_as_printed: of the 42 patients with chemosensory dysfunction, 64% reported a complete and 19% a near complete recovery at follow-up (combined olfactory/gustatory, as printed)
recovery_any_as_printed: 83% of the 42 symptomatic patients reported a complete or near complete recovery at follow-up (combined OD/GD, as printed); a partial recovery (30–50 points) from GD was reported by 4/42 patients after a mean of 32 days; 3 patients reported no improvement of both ageusia and anosmia after a mean of 27 days
time_to_recovery_as_printed: mean duration of GD 16 days (mean duration of OD 18 days); mean recovery time from OD or GD significantly longer for females than males (26 vs 14 days, P = 0.009)
pathogenesis_finding: Bradykinin hypothesis: reduced ACE/ACE2 activity after SARS-CoV-2 binding increases bradykinin and [des-Arg9]-bradykinin; "BK seems also involved in GD, through a neurogenic inflammatory mechanism or an excess of activity directly in the central nervous system", and bradykinin can activate TRPA1 on trigeminal neurons projecting to the tongue; ACE2 is noted to be diffusely expressed on the oral mucosa, particularly the tongue
special_populations_notes: older adults: hospitalized cohort with mean age 65 years (range 29–94) — the paper's stated focus on an older population
follow_up_duration: approximately 1 month after discharge (single telephone follow-up of patients discharged a month earlier)
funding_conflicts: Funding: none; conflicts: "The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest"
extractor_notes: The five basic taste qualities were not individually investigated. Recovery percentages are printed for combined olfactory/gustatory dysfunction; GD-specific items (partial recovery in 4/42; mean GD duration 16 days) are recorded as printed. No intervention tested.

design: other (case report, n=1 — below the >=10 case-series threshold, flag, do not extract as primary)
country_setting: USA; hospital emergency department (Abington Hospital–Jefferson Health, Abington)
population_description: Single case: 60-year-old woman presenting with right-sided headache (attributed to trigeminal neuralgia) with concurrent anosmia and ageusia, without fever or respiratory symptoms; history of asthma, vertigo, seasonal allergies and anxiety
taste_types_reported: ageusia; dysgeusia (metallic taste in the mouth)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (clinical history)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported
onset_timing: anosmia and ageusia present at presentation, with headache for the past week (as printed)
pathogenesis_finding: "There are a few hypothesized mechanisms of action on why COVID-19 patients may develop anosmia and ageusia... It could be due to direct damage of the virus on olfactory and gustatory receptors"
special_populations_notes: older adults: patient aged 60 years
funding_conflicts: funding not reported; conflicts: "The authors have declared that no competing interests exist"
extractor_notes: Single case report — excluded from synthesis by the locked protocol (case reports <10) but extracted here as included in the pool. Gabapentin 300 mg twice daily was prescribed for trigeminal neuralgia headache, not for taste dysfunction — no intervention tested for taste. Sustentacular-cell (ACE2/TMPRSS2) discussion is olfactory-specific — not Q2-coded per R5.

country_setting: Poland; nonhospitalized COVID-19 patients in home-based isolation (nationwide survey)
population_description: Nonhospitalized patients with laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 in home-based isolation (mild-to-moderate disease); median age 50 years; 60.2% women
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (8-question telephone survey: "During your illness, did you have... taste disorder?")
taste_prevalence_as_printed: taste disorder in 923/1942 (47.5%) overall; women 617/1169 (52.8%) vs men 306/773 (39.6%), P<0.001; at least one olfactory or taste disorder in 54.2% and both alterations in 42.5% of patients
pathogenesis_theories: T11 (hormonal modulation of the gustatory system, proposed to explain sex differences)
pathogenesis_finding: "Moreover, the impact of hormonal modulation on the gustatory system should be considered" (raised, with sex differences in olfactory bulb neurons/glial cells, to explain the higher frequency of taste disorders in women)
special_populations_notes: diabetes: diabetes in 88/1942 respondents (4.5%)
funding_conflicts: Conflicts: none declared; funding not reported
extractor_notes: Symptoms were self-reported and not physician-confirmed; taste was a single yes/no item with no subtype or severity grading. No intervention tested.

country_setting: Germany; München Klinik Schwabing, Munich (hospital cohort — the first COVID-19 patients in Germany, "Webasto cluster")
N_total: hospitalized COVID-19 patients 63 ; reported loss of smell and/or taste 26 ; smell-tested 14 ; taste-tested 10
population_description: Patients hospitalized with COVID-19 between 27 January and 21 March 2020; the 26 patients reporting chemosensory dysfunction comprised 13 women and 13 men, age range 15–85 years, mean age 46 years (SD 15)
taste_types_reported: unspecified taste disorder (patient-reported loss of taste, not separated from smell in the cohort report)
taste_measurement: psychophysical test ("Taste Strips" test of the 4 basic taste qualities, performed in 10 patients, before and after nasal decongestion with xylometazoline 0.1% spray) plus spontaneous patient report
taste_prevalence_as_printed: loss of sense of smell and/or taste reported by 26/63 patients (41%) (combined, as printed); no separate taste-loss prevalence reported; on taste testing all 10 tested patients recognised at least 3 of the 4 taste qualities, i.e. normal gustatory function — "There were no indications of an increased incidence of dysgeusia"
recovery_any_as_printed: all tested patients reported an improvement ("Besserung") of smell and/or taste within 8–23 days after onset of the first COVID-19 symptoms (combined smell/taste, as printed; one patient was unreachable in the further course)
time_to_recovery_as_printed: improvement of smell and/or taste within 8–23 days (mean 13.9 days, SD 5.3) after onset of first symptoms
pathogenesis_finding: Because taste-strip testing was normal in all tested patients, the authors conclude it is likely that patients confused gustatory function with retronasal olfactory function when complaining of loss of the sense of taste ("Es liegt daher nahe, dass die Patienten die gustatorische Funktion und die retronasale olfaktorische Funktion verwechselten")
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Conflicts: all authors declare no conflict of interest ("kein Interessenkonflikt"); funding not reported
extractor_notes: Article in German with English abstract; extraction from both. Xylometazoline nasal spray was used only as a test procedure (decongestion before/after comparison), not as a treatment for taste loss — no Q3 intervention. Repeat smell/taste testing was possible in only 4 of 14 tested patients (2–6 days after the first test).

design: other (systematic review — no primary data, flag, do not extract as primary)
country_setting: not reported
N_total: studies included 24 (18 reviewed articles ; 6 manuscript preprints)
population_description: Published studies and preprints (to 3 May 2020) reporting sudden anosmia/taste loss in the context of COVID-19 infection; no primary patient population
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Conflicts: "The authors have no conflicts of interest"; funding not reported
extractor_notes: Systematic review of 24 studies/preprints on smell and taste disorders in suspected COVID-19; most included studies reported smell loss or smell plus taste loss, and the review's Table 1 figures are other studies' data — not extracted here per R1(d)-style flag for secondary evidence. No intervention tested.

design: cross-sectional | (paper's wording: "Prospective, cross-sectional" telephone questionnaire study)
country_setting: Switzerland; Kantonsspital Aarau (regional/cantonal hospital)
population_description: Patients diagnosed with COVID-19 at Kantonsspital Aarau between 3 March and 17 April 2020 who could be reached by telephone (ICU patients and deceased excluded); mean age 46.8 years (SD 15.9); 48.5% male; 4 were inpatients and 19 previously hospitalized at interview, the rest outpatients
taste_types_reported: hypogeusia; ageusia (as printed: sense of taste rated "decreased" or "none at all" at its worst)
taste_measurement: patient-reported scale (standardised telephone questionnaire; sense of taste rated normal/decreased/none at all versus baseline, and severity at its worst on a 0–3 scale [none/mild/moderate/severe] modelled on the validated nasal symptom score)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: gustatory dysfunction in 65.0% (95% CI 55.5–73.6) of 103 patients: sense of taste "decreased" in 25.2% (95% CI 17.8–34.4) and "none at all" in 39.8% (95% CI 30.9–49.5) at its worst; among patients reporting some taste loss, severity was mild in 10.4%, moderate in 22.4% and severe in 67.2%; severity of loss of taste strongly correlated with severity of olfactory dysfunction (ρ = 0.87, P < .001)
onset_timing: not reported for taste (onset day was asked for decreased smell and taste, but timing results are printed for olfactory dysfunction only: median day 3)
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: Dr Speth and Dr Singer-Cornelius received funding from Kantonsspital Aarau, Department of Otolaryngology, funded by Research Council KSA 1410.000.128; competing interests: none; sponsorships: none
extractor_notes: Mean severity score for decreased sense of taste was 1.7 (SD 1.3) (a worst-point level, not a change). Interviews occurred a median of 11 days after symptom onset, while most patients were still in the infection course; resolution was explicitly not studied. Discussion of ACE2 expression and coronavirus neurotropism concerns the nasal/olfactory route — not taste-extended, not Q2-coded per R5. No intervention tested.

country_setting: Italy; primary care (Puglia)
population_description: Patients swabbed for suspected COVID-19 in primary care in Puglia, Italy; mean age 49.7 years (range 19-70); analysis restricted to the 72 PCR-positive patients
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no
taste_prevalence_as_printed: isolated dysgeusia 18 (25%); anosmia and dysgeusia 34 (47%); isolated anosmia 8 (11%); neither 12 (17%) - of 72 PCR-positive patients, as printed
onset_timing: sensory symptoms preceded respiratory symptoms in 45 (75%); mean latent period 2.8 days (range 1-4)
recovery_complete_as_printed: taste-specific not reported; composite sensory symptoms: completely disappeared 22 (37%)
recovery_any_as_printed: composite sensory symptoms: completely disappeared 22 (37%) or partially disappeared 20 (33%), as printed
time_to_recovery_as_printed: mean duration of sensory symptoms 16.1 days (range 7-22) - composite smell/taste, as printed
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: sensory symptoms unchanged in 18 (30%) at assessment (<12wk - not >=12wk persistence)
pathogenesis_theories: T11 (swiftly disappearing neurotoxic effect and/or cytopathic damage, as hypothesised)
pathogenesis_finding: The authors hypothesised a swiftly disappearing neurotoxic effect and/or cytopathic damage to explain the sensory symptoms.
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported; Conflicts: each author declares no commercial associations that might pose a conflict of interest
extractor_notes: Recovery figures are composite (smell and taste combined) as printed; no taste-specific recovery reported. A combined dysgeusia total is not printed and was not computed.

country_setting: France; hospital outpatients (Nord Franche-Comte Hospital)
virus_confirmation: laboratory-confirmed (RT-PCR, nasopharyngeal; Charite E gene / Pasteur RdRp)
population_description: Adults aged >=18 years presenting to hospital for possible COVID-19, compared by RT-PCR result (positive vs negative)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (standardised questionnaire)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: dysgeusia in PCR-positive 62 (65.3%) vs PCR-negative 19 (15.6%); dysgeusia with anosmia 52 vs 11, as printed
special_populations_notes: Pregnant women, children and patients with dementia were excluded
follow_up_duration: not reported (outcomes of hospitalised patients not collected)
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported; Conflicts: no competing interests declared
extractor_notes: No recovery, persistence, score-change or pathogenesis data reported.

country_setting: USA; hospital/ICU (Philadelphia)
population_description: 59-year-old African-American female hospitalised with COVID-19 pneumonia
taste_measurement: self-report symptom (clinical history)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported (single case)
onset_timing: taste symptoms began about a week before admission, as an initial symptom preceding respiratory symptoms
pathogenesis_finding: The case discussion attributes the taste disturbance in part to anosmia/retronasal flavour loss affecting taste perception.
special_populations_notes: none reported
follow_up_duration: not reported (course reported to discharge, 10 days after admission)
funding_conflicts: Funding: no specific grant declared; Conflicts: none declared
extractor_notes: At discharge (8 April 2020) taste was 'greatly improved' but with lingering dysgeusia - improvement wording not labelled recovery (R3), quoted here verbatim; foods described as 'bland and metallic', later 'excessively salty'. Hydroxychloroquine, azithromycin, steroids and CPAP were given for COVID-19 pneumonia, not for taste dysfunction - not coded as an intervention (R6).

country_setting: South Korea; Daegu cohort (community/hospital)
N_total: total 3,191; asymptomatic-to-mild subgroup 2,342; followed for anosmia 232; followed for ageusia 196 (discussion states 143 followed for ageusia - internal discrepancy as printed)
population_description: Confirmed COVID-19 patients in Daegu, Korea, mostly asymptomatic-to-mild, surveyed by telephone with follow-up calls for symptom duration
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (telephone interview); prevalence reported as composite anosmia-or-ageusia
taste_prevalence_as_printed: composite anosmia or ageusia 488/3,191 (15.3%); in the asymptomatic-to-mild subgroup 367/2,342 (15.7%); taste-specific prevalence not reported separately
time_to_recovery_as_printed: median time to recovery of ageusia 7 days, as printed; duration of ageusia median 6.0 days (IQR 3.0-10.0) in the follow-up table
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: most patients with ageusia recovered within 3 weeks (<12wk - not >=12wk persistence)
pathogenesis_finding: ACE2 is widely expressed on oral mucosal epithelial cells and damage to these cells may explain ageusia; ageusia may also be a secondary result of olfactory dysfunction.
special_populations_notes: Diabetes 164/3,191 (5.1%); immunosuppressant use 35 (1.1%); age over 60 years 658 (20.6%) - cohort characteristics as printed
follow_up_duration: not reported (telephone follow-up until symptom resolution)
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported; Conflicts: authors have no potential conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Taste-specific prevalence is not separable from the composite anosmia-or-ageusia figure as printed.

country_setting: Italy; multicentre
population_description: COVID-19 patients in an ongoing multicentre Italian study; preliminary report published as a letter
taste_measurement: other-as-stated: objective functional chemosensitive evaluation protocol (instrument not named in the letter)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: composite only: chemosensitive disorders in about 80% of patients; taste and/or smell disturbances the sole manifestation in 15.3%
onset_timing: generally 2 days after onset of fever
recovery_any_as_printed: composite: symptoms spontaneously regressed within a few days in 67.5% (smell/taste combined, as printed)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: chemosensitive alteration lasting more than 10 days reported (<12wk - not >=12wk persistence)
pathogenesis_finding: The authors suggest non-neuronal targets (supporting cells of the chemosensitive epithelia) rather than neuronal death underlie the chemosensitive disorders.
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported; Conflicts: 'We have no conflicts of interest'
extractor_notes: Letter reporting preliminary results of an ongoing study; taste is not separable from smell for prevalence or recovery (composite as printed). A qualitative increase in taste thresholds is described but no score change is quantified.

design: other (narrative review - flag, do not extract as primary)
country_setting: not reported
population_description: not reported
taste_measurement: not reported
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported
special_populations_notes: none reported
funding_conflicts: Funding: no financial support; Conflicts: none declared
extractor_notes: Narrative review - flag, do not extract as primary. Mechanisms discussed (nasal mucosal inflammation obstructing airflow; viral disruption of olfactory mucosa in post-viral olfactory dysfunction) are olfactory-only - general/olfactory mechanism not taste-extended - not Q2-coded (R5). Steroids are discussed for olfactory post-viral dysfunction only, not for taste - no intervention coded (R6).

country_setting: 12 European hospitals (Belgium, France, Spain, Italy and others)
N_total: completed study 417; gustatory prevalence assessed 385 (32 who did not remember excluded)
population_description: Adults over 18 years with mild-to-moderate COVID-19; patients with pre-existing olfactory/gustatory dysfunction and ICU patients excluded
taste_measurement: patient-reported questionnaire (based on the NHANES smell and taste component)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: gustatory dysfunction 88.0% (abstract) / 342 (88.8%) of 385 (results) - both as printed; of those affected, reduced/discontinued function 78.9% and distorted function 21.1%
recovery_complete_as_printed: taste-specific not reported; composite: 25.5% recovered both olfactory and gustatory functions throughout the 2 weeks after resolution of general symptoms
special_populations_notes: Pre-existing olfactory/gustatory dysfunction excluded
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported; Conflicts: authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Gustatory dysfunction was treated in 1.4% (4 patients; L-carnitine or trace elements/vitamins) with no outcomes reported - not an intervention tested for taste (R6). Mechanisms discussed are olfactory (olfactory bulb/CNS invasion; ACE2 population susceptibility) - general/olfactory mechanism not taste-extended - not Q2-coded (R5).

country_setting: USA; clinics in Kalamazoo, MI and Los Angeles, CA
population_description: Patients enrolled with ageusia and anosmia after COVID-19 and treated with the TNT protocol (enrolment conditional on chemosensory dysfunction)
taste_measurement: other-as-stated: qualitative yes/no detection panel of 4 taste agents (sugar, salt, lemon juice, orange bitters), scored as % detected
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: gustatory dysfunction 5/5 (enrolment required ageusia with anosmia)
onset_timing: positive detection on average 4.2 days after symptom onset (range 0-8) as printed in text; Table 2 labels 4.2 (range 0-8) as time from symptoms until TNT initiated - discrepancy as printed
taste_score_change_as_printed: whole cohort (n=5): mean taste detection score 10% at baseline, about 58% at about 10 days (p=0.0002), and 100% at final evaluation (p<0.0001 vs baseline)
pathogenesis_finding: The authors propose ACE2-mediated infection of taste bud cells causing apoptosis/receptor degradation and decreased sensitivity, with inflammation (TNF-alpha) and salivary gland damage also contributing.
intervention: Comprehensive 'Training 'N' Treatment' (TNT) protocol (multicomponent: supplements, saline irrigation, fluticasone, sensory training, nerve stimulation exercises; phase 2 topical/systemic steroids and sprays for partial recovery)
intervention_dose_course: Zinc 50 mg daily; vitamin A 10,000 IU daily; vitamin D3 10,000 IU daily; alpha lipoic acid 300-600 mg twice daily; B-complex (B6 100 mg, B12 100 mcg); saline nasal irrigation twice daily; fluticasone spray; taste sensory training 3x daily and smell training 4x daily; chorda tympani and trigeminal nerve stimulation exercises. Phase 2 (partial recovery): triamcinolone dental paste (0.01% in Table 1; 0.1% applied twice daily for 1 hour in methods - discrepancy as printed), sodium citrate spray, theophylline spray, prednisone 60 mg/day for 10 days
treatment_recovery_as_printed: complete recovery of taste (and smell) in every patient (5/5, 100%); all complete by day 37; 4 of 5 recovered by day 20; evaluations at about 10 and about 17 days
adverse_events_as_printed: No adverse events were reported during treatment with the TNT protocol.
special_populations_notes: Non-stable autoimmune disease, psychiatric disorder and steroid/anti-inflammatory use were exclusions
funding_conflicts: Funding: Private Health Management, Inc. and Simon Medical Services, PC; Conflicts: none declared
extractor_notes: Preprint (Research Square). The paper self-labels a retrospective case series; the IRB protocol title describes a retrospective cohort analysis. TNT is also stated to have been initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset/positive test, conflicting with the 4.2-day figure - both as printed.

country_setting: Switzerland; Emergency Unit, Cantonal Hospital of Riaz, Fribourg
N_total: arrived/monitored 221; analysed 118 (39 COVID-positive; 79 COVID-negative selected as controls)
population_description: Patients aged 17-90 years with mild-to-moderate respiratory symptoms presenting to the emergency unit, April-October 2020; COVID-positive patients vs randomly selected COVID-negative controls
taste_measurement: patient-reported scale (0-10 self-evaluation of gustatory function; 0 = ageusia, 10 = normogeusia)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: poorer taste sensitivity (score 0-5) in 30% of COVID-positive vs 13% of COVID-negative patients; sweet changes 41% vs 14%, salty 38% vs 15%, bitter 23% vs 13%, sour 23% vs 13% (discussion reports dysgeusia 35% vs 13% - variant as printed)
pathogenesis_finding: The acute cytokine storm and mucus hypersecretion might affect nasal flow and result in the associated olfactory and gustatory disturbances.
special_populations_notes: Pregnancy excluded; moderate-to-severe respiratory disease excluded
funding_conflicts: Funding: intramural funding from Cantonal Hospital of Fribourg and the Swiss Integrative Center for Human Health; Conflicts: no known competing financial interests
extractor_notes: Preprint (medRxiv). Group mean taste scores (6.51 +/- 3.74 COVID-positive vs 8.55 +/- 2.18 COVID-negative, p=0.003) are a between-group difference, not a validated score change, so field 17 is 'not reported'. BSIT measured smell only.

country_setting: Germany (4 cases), USA (3), Venezuela (2), Bolivia (1); case series
population_description: Case series of 10 patients diagnosed with viral-associated olfactory and taste loss (COVID-19)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom (clinical history/anamnesis)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: ageusia 9/10; anosmia 8/10; both 7/10 - as printed
onset_timing: ageusia presented a median of 2 days after symptom onset; on days 1-2 in 5 patients, days 4-5 in 3 patients, day 10 in 1 patient
time_to_recovery_as_printed: ageusia persisted a median of 8 days (range 4-25)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: ageusia durations up to 25 days (<12wk - not >=12wk persistence)
pathogenesis_finding: The authors state ageusia in these patients is most probably secondary to a diminished taste perception as a consequence of anosmia; direct viral sensorineural injury cannot be entirely excluded.
special_populations_notes: Patient 7 systemic lupus erythematosus; patient 8 type 2 diabetes; patient 10 adult Still's disease; patient 1 aged 86 years - as printed
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported; Conflicts: no competing interests, except authors JM and MPTT are patients 5 and 10 of the series

country_setting: USA; online registry (42 states; Brigham, Boston, MA)
N_total: screened/enrolled 587; eligible/analysed 426; clinical measurement subset (UPSIT + B-WETT) 74, plus 20 healthy controls
virus_confirmation: mixed (physician diagnosis, or positive PCR, or antigen test)
population_description: Adults aged >=18 years with a COVID-19 history and loss/changes in smell and/or taste for at least 1 week, enrolled in an online registry with follow-up questionnaires at 3, 6 and 12 months
taste_measurement: self-report study questionnaires; validated gustatory test (B-WETT) in the clinical measurement subset
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: composite chronic olfactory and/or gustatory dysfunction 362 (85%) lasting 1-24 months without significant improvement; recovered 64 (15%)
recovery_any_as_printed: composite: 64 (15%) regained at least 80% of smell and/or taste function, as printed
time_to_recovery_as_printed: composite: symptom duration in the recovered group 2.8 +/- 3 months vs 7.4 +/- 5 months in the chronic group, as printed
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: chronic olfactory and/or gustatory dysfunction lasting 1-24 months, as printed (composite)
pathogenesis_theories: T11 (nose/mouth dryness proposed as a contributor; nasal lining fluid/tastant transport)
pathogenesis_finding: Persistent dysfunction was not associated with subjective nasal inflammation (SNOT-22 <20); nose/mouth dryness was proposed as a contributor to persistent dysgeusia.
special_populations_notes: Diabetes and chronic kidney disease each in <10% of participants, as printed
funding_conflicts: not reported
extractor_notes: Preprint (medRxiv). Registry subgroups as printed: dysosmia n=24, subjective dysosmia n=9, dysgeusia n=4, dysosmia+dysgeusia n=10, recovered n=3, congenital anosmia n=2 (clinical subset). Treatments tried were reported descriptively for smell only (systemic steroids - only 6% reported improvement; olfactory training marginally more effective) - no taste intervention tested (R6). B-WETT results reported with p-values/figures only, no numeric change printed.

country_setting: Switzerland; laboratory study (Lausanne)
